body_markdown:
# Adam Francis Telfer (1842–1925)

**Role:** Scottish migrant who followed his brothers to Australia — the Tantanoola pioneer

**Born:** 14 September 1842 — Jedburgh, Roxburghshire, Scotland
**Died:** 12 January 1925 — Knightsbridge, South Australia
**Occupation:** Shepherd, stockholder, storekeeper, grazier
**Spouse:** [[Margaret Dougal Telfer (1849–1936)]] (m. 25 March 1868)

---

## Family

| Relation | Name |
|----------|------|
| **Mother** | Elizabeth Beattie |
| **Father** | James Telfer |
| **Spouse** | [[Margaret Dougal Telfer (1849–1936)]] |
| **Cousin / Uncle** | [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]] |

---

## Family Stories

### The Ship That Sank

Adam was born at Jedburgh, Roxburghshire, Scotland on 14th September 1842, the youngest son of James and Elizabeth Telfer. His father died in 1863 from injuries in an agricultural accident — a hard blow for the family. Adam made the difficult decision to leave his mother and sisters behind and follow his brothers to South Australia. He sailed on the steamer "London" on her second voyage, a 140-day journey from Gravesend to Melbourne. The ship's master was J.B. Martin. On the shipping list, some rushed clerk wrote Adam's nationality as "Irish" — a Scot through and through. The "London" sank on her next voyage. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.267)*

### Overland to Uncle Francis

Adam landed in Melbourne and travelled overland to South Australia, making contact with his Uncle Francis at "Macoota", Kersbrook, and the brothers and sister who'd come before him. He worked as a shepherd and spent some time with his eldest brother James at Koppio Station near Port Lincoln. Rough country, lonely work — the kind that made a man of you. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.267)*

### Marrying His Cousin

In 1868, Adam returned to Kersbrook and married his cousin, Margaret Dougal Telfer — the daughter of his Uncle Francis. She was just 18, he was 25. The wedding was at her father's home, "Macoota". He was listed as a "Stockholder, of Koppio, Port Lincoln." After the wedding they went back to Koppio for several years. It was a marriage that would last 57 years and produce twelve children. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.267-268)*

### The Tantanoola Store

In the early 1870s, Adam and Margaret moved to the South East of South Australia. Adam's first community appointment was as Vice President of the Millicent Show in 1878. In 1880, he opened a store in Tantanoola — then known as Lucieton. The country was booming: the soil "will grow anything," the town was laid out with "excellent judgement," and the white stone buildings showed through the foliage "to great advantage." The Telfers were among those pioneers building it all. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.269-272)*

### The Farewell at Tantanoola Station

After 28 years in Tantanoola, Adam and Margaret left in 1908. The district presented them with a silver tea service — still held by their great-grandson Bruce Watson of Millicent as of 1986. When the train arrived, friends gathered on the platform and sang "God be with you till we meet again." It was too much for daughter Eva, who grabbed her son Rex and boarded the train before anyone saw her cry. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.272-275)*

### Edgerston House

The family settled at "Waverley Park" in Lower Mitcham, then moved to "Edgerston House" on Rochester Street, Knightsbridge in 1916. The nine-roomed house had large grounds with a creek meandering through the garden, a wooden bridge covered in wisteria, an extensive orchard, and stables. The family joined the Knightsbridge Baptist Church, the girls taught Sunday School, and Hazel sang in the choir. During the First World War, Adam wrote to his son Frank about the Irish Blight ruining the potatoes and the British Government wanting all the wool. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.274-275)*

### The Stroke

In 1919, Adam suffered a stroke. He recovered some function but his left arm and hand were useless, and his sight was failing. He wrote letters anyway, joking about it: "I have written such a long list of letters today so think I will finish up with one to you. I have written to Ted, Frank, Ray, Tom Holloway and Elsie at Broken Hill, and now if I write one to you that will be na sae bad for a blind man." His wife Margaret would finish the letters for him: "Father has left this so I will close it for him." *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.275-276)*

### The Smith Brothers' Return

In 1920, Adam wrote to Effie about the return of Sir Ross and Sir Keith Smith to Adelaide after their epic flight from England. "There was about 20,000 people to meet them. Mother and I saw them come over Mount Lofty but we did not leave the verandah to see them." He also complained of lumbago and a dry season: "Our garden does not look well. The trees are nearly dead for the want of rain but I think they will get over it if only we get plenty of rain." The old Scot, still tending his garden even as his health failed. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.276)*

### Adam's Death

Margaret nursed Adam for six years after his stroke. He died on 12th January 1925 at age 82. The Advertiser ran a death notice, and The Chronicle published an obituary noting his arrival on the "London" and his forty years of grazing in the South East. He left a widow, four sons, seven daughters, and 28 grandchildren. Margaret lived another eleven years. Both are buried at Mitcham Cemetery, with the words "God is our Refuge and Strength" — from Margaret's favourite Psalm 46 — on the headstone. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.276-277)*

---

## Life Story

Adam Francis Telfer was born at Jedburgh, Scotland in 1842. After his father's death in an agricultural accident, he emigrated to Australia on the steamer "London" — which sank on her next voyage. He worked as a shepherd at Koppio Station before marrying his cousin Margaret Dougal Telfer in 1868. They raised twelve children, first at Koppio, then at Tantanoola where Adam opened a store. The family moved to Adelaide in 1908 and settled at Knightsbridge. Adam suffered a stroke in 1919 and died in 1925.

**Source:** *From the Borders to the Bush* — pages 267-277

title: Adam Telfer — Family & Biography
body_markdown:
Born ~1771 at Sorbietrees, Roxburghshire, Scotland. Son of James Telfer and Margaret Armstrong of Sorbietrees. Died 6 February 1846 at Newcastleton aged 75. Name on family headstone in Castleton Cemetery. The name "Adam" appears regularly in succeeding Telfer generations.

## Family Stories

### The Brother on the Headstone

Most of what we know about Adam Telfer comes from one place: a headstone in Castleton Cemetery, Newcastleton. It reads:

> "Erected in Memory of Francis Telfer, who died at Newcastleton on 4th June, 1836, aged 68 years (b 1768). Also Jenet Telfer, his sister, who died at Newcastleton on 9th February 1842, aged 72 years (b 1770). Also Adam Telfer, their brother, who died at Newcastleton on 6th February, 1846, aged 75 years (b 1771)."

That's it. Three siblings on one stone — Francis, Jenet, and Adam — all dying within a decade of each other, all in the same little border town. Adam never married (or if he did, no record survived). He never left Scotland. He lived his whole life within a few miles of where he was born, in the Liddesdale valley near the English border.

But here's the thing. The name "Adam" didn't die with him. It kept popping up in the family for generations — Adam Telfer (1799–?), Adam Francis Telfer (1842–1925), and further down the line. Some names travel better than people do.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.17-19; Castleton Cemetery headstone)*

**Source:** *From the Borders to the Bush* — pages 17-19; Castleton Cemetery headstone

body_markdown:
# Adam Telfer (1799–?)

**Role:** Brother of Francis Telfer (1809–1895)

Adam Telfer was born on 18 October 1799 at Greenholm, near Newcastleton, Roxburghshire, Scotland. He was the fourth child of James Telfer (1761–1845), a hand loom weaver, and Elizabeth "Betty" Hutton (1774–1853).

His baptism was recorded in the Old Parish Register of Castleton (Volume 784/1) as: "1799 October 18 — Adam to James Telfer and Betty Hutton at Greenholm."

The family later moved from Greenholm to Blackburnfoot, at the northern end of Newcastleton, where two more children were born. Blackburnfoot had its own weaving industry, and the cottage where his brother Francis was born still stood into the 1980s.

The book states: *"We have no further information about four members of this family; namely Isobel, Adam, Margaret and William."* Like his older sister Isobel and younger siblings Margaret and William, Adam's fate after the family records is not documented.

He is one of the "Other Children" on the family tree, distinguished from his nephew Adam (1796–1863, son of James Telfer and Elizabeth Beattie).

**Source:** *From the Borders to the Bush* — pages 17–20

---

## Family Stories

### The Lost Thread

Adam Telfer was born on 18 October 1799 at Greenholm, near Newcastleton — the fourth child of James Telfer, a hand loom weaver, and Elizabeth Hutton. The family moved to Blackburnfoot, where the cottage his brother Francis was born in still stood into the 1980s.

And then the thread goes cold. The book puts it plainly: *"We have no further information about four members of this family; namely Isobel, Adam, Margaret and William."* Adam's fate after the family records ends is not documented.

He's one of the ghosts of the family tree — a name in the parish register, a son of the Scottish Borders, whose life was lived beyond the reach of the record book.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.17-20)*

# Alan Dale Telfer (1890–1937)

**Born:** 27 Oct 1890 (Tantanoola, SA) | **Died:** 13 Sep 1937 (Wilga Tank, Girilambone, NSW) | **Mother:** [[Martha Henstridge (~1854–1921)]] | **Father:** [[John Telfer (1840–1913)]] | **Occupation:** Coalminer / Ganger (railway labor) | **Buried:** Unknown (Girilambone district)

## Family

## Life Summary

Alan Dale Telfer was born on 27 October 1890 in Tantanoola, South Australia, the 13th child of John Telfer (1840–1913) and his second wife Martha Clara Henstridge.

He never married. During the Great Depression of the 1920s-1930s, Alan migrated far from the agricultural safety of South Australia's Limestone Coast to the interior of New South Wales. He found work as a **ganger** (railway labor foreman) and **coalminer** — a gruelling and highly itinerant profession that took him deep into the state's central-west.

### Death — Resolved (NSW Government Gazette)

Alan's fate was a long-standing mystery in the Telfer family tree. The resolution came via an NSW Government Gazette intestate estate notice, which confirmed:

> Alan Dale Telfer, late of **Wilga Tank, Girilambone**, in the State of New South Wales, died **intestate** on **13 September 1937**.

Girilambone and the associated Wilga Tank area was a remote railway siding and copper mining outpost in central-western New South Wales. His death there, without a will, paints a picture of a rugged, transient, and likely impoverished life in his final years — a stark contrast to the settled farming life of his Tantanoola siblings.

His exact burial location is unknown but likely in the Girilambone district.

## Family Stories

Alan Dale was born at Tantanoola in 1890, the 13th child of John Telfer (1840–1913) and Martha Henstridge. The family history records him as "Allan Dale (1890–1955)" in the family tree. He never married. During the Great Depression he migrated to New South Wales, finding work as a ganger (railway labour foreman) and coalminer. He died intestate at Wilga Tank, Girilambone, a remote railway siding in central-western New South Wales, on 13 September 1937 — a rugged end far from the settled farming life of his Tantanoola siblings. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.258)*

## Family Stories

Albert George Telfer was the fifth child of John and Caroline Telfer, born on 14 November 1881 at Angle Farm, near Hawker. His birth came at a time when the family was establishing their home — a well had been sunk providing permanent water for stock and household use, and they were harvesting their fourth crop. In 1903, when his father purchased the Warcowie homestead, Albert took over its management, beginning a long farming career.

Albert was a farmer with a keen interest in examining new ideas and learning from them. He became a foundation member of the Warcowie Agricultural Bureau and took an active part in its activities. He married Beatrice Rowe, and their children — Rita Joyce, Beatrice Sylvia, Douglas Ivan, Melville Bruce, John Alick Ralph and Murray Keith — were all born while the family lived at Warcowie.

In 1923, Albert bought a farm at Hill River, six miles east of Clare, so that his children could attend the High School there. Farming at Clare, one of the wetter areas of the state, was very different from the drier conditions he had been accustomed to at Hawker. His first crop at Hill River was quite good, but 80 acres were destroyed by a severe hailstorm. Despite such setbacks, Albert and Beatrice built a new life at Clare, and their family grew and prospered there.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.144–146)*

## Photos

![Francis Charles 'Charlie' Telfer and Amy Ellen Provis on their wedding day, 6 April 1909](../_assets/Francis Charles and Amy Telfer wedding 6 April 1909.jpg)

*Francis Charles 'Charlie' Telfer (aged 33) and Amy Ellen Provis (aged 25) on their wedding day, 6 April 1909, at Stokes, South Australia. Studio portrait in sepia tones. Charlie in dark three-piece suit with handlebar moustache, white pocket square, gold watch chain, and floral boutonnière. Amy in elaborate white lace gown with high ruffled collar, voluminous sleeves, and floral headpiece, holding a small bouquet. Painted tropical foliage backdrop and heavy draped curtain — classic studio setting of the era.*

![Telfer family reunion, circa 1920](../_assets/Telfer family reunion c1920.jpg)

*Telfer family reunion, circa 1920. Large multi-generational group portrait of ~25 individuals. Amy Ellen Telfer (1884–1951, aged ~36) standing among the adults with her husband Francis Charles 'Charlie' Telfer (1875–1954, aged ~45), their children and grandchildren. Her parents-in-law John Telfer (1847–1929, aged ~73) and Caroline Amelia Telfer (1842–1929, aged ~78) seated center with white beard and lace collar respectively. Studio setting with textured wallpaper backdrop on left, dark curtain on right.*

> 
> ![Amy ellen telfer grave](images/people/amy-ellen-telfer-grave.jpg)

---

## Family Stories

Amy Ellen Provis married Francis Charles Telfer at Stokes in 1909 and together they raised ten children on a pioneering farm at Ungarra on the Eyre Peninsula. Life was brutally hard for her — no electricity, no running water, no refrigeration, no washing machine. She cooked on a wood stove, baked all the family's bread using homemade yeast made from hops, potatoes, flour and water, and made butter that she had to drive 18 miles into Tumby Bay in a sulky with one horse before the heat of the day. The money from the butter bought whatever groceries she could manage. She did the family laundry with a copper that had to be stoked with wood, two tubs, a scrubbing board and homemade soap, and ironed with a box iron full of hot coals. She carried water from the sheds in four-gallon kerosene tin buckets for all household needs. With a baby every couple of years, she somehow kept the household running through it all. Her daughters remembered that there was no entertainment as such in those days, "but plenty of hard work and just enough rest to keep us going." *(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.130–131)*

On **6 April 1909**, she married [[Francis Charles Telfer (1875–1954)]] at Stokes, South Australia. The wedding was reportedly covered by a local newspaper article — "Family Wedding at Jamestown" — which mentions the celebration.

Together they raised **ten children** on family farms, moving from the mid-north toward the Eyre Peninsula over the decades. Amy passed away in October 1951, predeceasing her husband Francis by about three years.

Her name appears in Murray John Telfer's profile as "Amy May" in some vault records, but her registered birth name is **Amy Ellen Provis**.

---

## Parents: The Provis & Thorpe Families

**George Provis** (Amy's father) — married **Emily Ellen Thorpe** on 15 June 1882. Emily's parents were **Charles Robert Thorpe** (1832–1893) and **Amelia White** (1833–1916).

title: Bertha Telfer — Family & Biography
body_markdown:
## Family Stories

Bertha was the adopted daughter of John and Caroline Telfer. As a child her mother died and her father — a Swiss immigrant named Moelling — could not care for his four children, so Bertha was taken in and raised by the Telfer family. She studied at Rev Lockhart Morton's College in Adelaide preparing for missionary service and was accepted by the United Aborigines Mission in December 1908. At the Burnt Bridge Mission on the Macleay River in 1906, she gave addresses alongside Mrs Rudder and Mrs Ingram. She was a tiny woman with enormous courage — the book describes her going to many places where a white woman had never been before, full of fun, with a simple faith. She would "just say a little prayer and the dear Lord will look after me." Around 1915–17 while at Sunday Island in the Buccaneer Archipelago near Broome, she met and married James Alcorn, an official with the Broome pearl fisheries. They had one son, Frank. After returning to South Australia and spending time at Willow Plains and Warcowie, they moved to New Guinea where Jim had a government job. They later lived at Clare and then Norwood, where they ran a small shop. After Jim's death, Bertha lived at Edwardstown in a granny flat built onto Frank's property until she became too feeble. She spent her remaining years at the Serene Nursing Home at Lockleys and died on 10 August 1965, aged 93. *(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.127–129)*

body_markdown:
# Caroline Amelia Telfer (1842–1929)

**Lifespan:** 10 June 1842 – 24 August 1929

**Branch:** Masters → Telfer (married into)

**Role:** School teacher at Tarlee; matriarch of Willow Plains; Mark's great-great-grandmother

## Biography

Caroline Amelia Masters was born 10th June 1842 in Brownsover, Warwickshire, England — daughter of Charles Masters and Martha Williams. She emigrated to South Australia with her family in July 1845 aboard the *Templar*.

The family farmed at Flaxman's Valley, Angaston. Her father Charles farmed there until about 1865, after which Martha (with the help of her children) carried on.

### The School Teacher

Caroline and her sister Mary Ellen first tried opening a school at Gilberton, near the Forrester's Arms Hotel — a staging camp for bullockies. The railway bypassed the hotel and the town of Tarlee sprang up at the rail head instead, so the venture failed.

In 1870 she tried again, granted a licence by the Tarlee District Council. She taught in the original section of the Baptist Church with 41 pupils — 18 boys and 23 girls. The Tarlee school history records her "dedication and persistence that would do a present day teacher proud." She taught there until 17th August 1874.

### Marriage and Family

She married [[John Telfer (1847–1929)]] on 22nd September 1874 in the Tarlee Baptist Church (her schoolroom for four years). She was 32, he was 27. John's brother George and Caroline's sister Mary Ellen were witnesses.

On the marriage certificate she signed as C.A. Masters. In later years she dropped the "Amelia" because she didn't want her initials to be C.A.T. Telfer. From then on she was C.M. Telfer.

### The Move North

When the government opened the Northern Districts for farming, it was Caroline who urged John to apply. After his successful application they moved to Arkaba, where she gave birth to six sons in a one-roomed wood and iron hut with a hessian partition. The first of these, Ernest John, was the first white baby born at Willow Plains.

She and John died within hours of each other in August 1929 — she on the 24th, he on the 23rd — and are buried together at Clare Cemetery.

## Family Stories

*See [[John Telfer (1847–1929)]] for full stories, including the uncle's matchmaking, the pupil's poem for baby John Ernest, the adopted children, the C.A.T. initials, Caroline's brick oven, and Cocky the wonder bird.*

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.109-118)*

title: Caroline (Masters) Telfer — Family & Biography
roles: Wife of John Telfer (1847–1929)
body_markdown:
# Caroline Masters (~1850–1929)

**Role:** Wife of John Telfer (1847–1929)

Caroline Masters married John Telfer (1847–1929), the eldest child of Francis Telfer and Margaret Wright. Together they raised a large family including Albert George, Ernest John, William James, Edwin Gilbert, Walter William, Maria Clara, and Caroline.

**Source:** *From the Borders to the Bush*

## Family Stories

Caroline Amelia Masters was the daughter of Charles Masters and Martha Williams of Flaxman's Valley, Angaston. Her father's family Bible, treasured by Caroline until her death and later passed to her youngest son Edwin, recorded the family's English origins in Brownsover, Warwickshire, and their emigration to South Australia in 1845. After her father died around 1868, Caroline and her sister Mary Ellen opened a school at Gilberton, next to the Forrester's Arms Hotel — a staging camp for bullockies hauling goods to and from Adelaide. But the venture failed when the railway bypassed the hotel and the population moved to the new rail head at Tarlee. In 1870 Caroline tried again, securing a licence from the Tarlee District Council. The book says she showed "dedication and persistence that would do a present day teacher proud," commencing classes in the original section of the Baptist Church with 41 pupils — 18 boys and 23 girls. This time her perseverance paid off and the school flourished. She taught there until 17 August 1874, when she resigned to marry John Telfer.

The match came about through the Flavel family. John's uncles, who lived at Finniss Point as close neighbours of Charles and Elizabeth Farrow, knew of the high esteem in which Miss Masters was held and felt she would make an excellent wife for a young pioneer. John took their advice, called on Miss Masters, and "seemed to have liked what he saw as he kept going back." They were married on 22 September 1874 at the Tarlee Baptist Church — her schoolroom for four years. On the marriage certificate Caroline signed as C.A. Masters, but she later dropped the "Amelia" to avoid her initials being C.A.T., signing as C.M. Telfer instead. Their first child Francis Charles was born in 1875, and a second son John Ernest in 1877 lived only six months before dying of pneumonia — Caroline wrote a poem at the time of his death.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.110–111)*

# Charles Farrow (~1836–1884)

**Role:** Husband of Elizabeth Hannah Telfer
**Born:** ~1836
**Died:** December 1884 — Pneumonia

Charles Farrow married Elizabeth Hannah Telfer. The book narrative records his death as December 1884 from pneumonia — 32 years before Elizabeth's death in 1916. (The chapter header shows 1828–1876, but the narrative text is the authoritative source.)

Together they had a large family including Peter, John, Charles, Esther Hannah, Elizabeth, Margaret, Sarah, Edith, James, Robert, William, and Eva Agnes Farrow.

**Source:** *From the Borders to the Bush* — Chapter on Elizabeth Hannah Telfer

## Family Stories

Charles Farrow married Elizabeth Telfer and the couple settled at Finniss Point, where they were close neighbours of the Flavel uncles who looked out for the young Telfer generation. It was these same uncles who knew of the high esteem in which the Tarlee schoolmistress Caroline Masters was held, and who steered young John Telfer her way — a chain of connections that ran right through the Farrow household at Finniss Point. Charles also stood as a witness at his sister-in-law Jane's second marriage to Frederick Parker, alongside his niece Jane Farrow, at the Wesleyan Church in Kapunda on Christmas Day 1871.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.93, 110)*

## Family Stories

Clarice May — known as May — was the eldest daughter of Francis Charles and Amy Telfer. She contributed a first-hand account of her father's pioneering life to the family history. She recalled how he drove his horses and wagon down from Hawker to the Eyre Peninsula to take up land, and described the gruelling childhood she and her siblings endured: walking three and a half miles to school each day, then coming home to feed hay into the chaff cutter by lantern light — "the prickles and mice it contained was not funny" — bagging up ten to twelve bags of chaff every night, tending sheep, milking cows, turning the milk separator, and pumping water by hand for the garden. # Dinah Flavel (1821–1844)

**Role:** Second wife of [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]] — mother of his daughter Jean
**Born:** 10 June 1821 — Pytchley, Kettering Borough, Northamptonshire, England
**Died:** 20 March 1844 (aged 22) — Chain of Ponds, Adelaide Hills, South Australia
**Buried:** West Terrace Cemetery, Adelaide, South Australia

## Family

| Relation | Name |
|----------|------|
| **Spouse** | [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]] (m. 4 May 1839) |
| **Daughter** | Jean Telfer (7 Aug 1840 – 15 Jul 1892) — m. A.F. Telfer |

## Life Summary

Dinah Flavel was born on 10 June 1821 at Pytchley, Northamptonshire, England — the daughter of Joseph Flavel (1797–1840) and Mary Bayes. Little is known of her childhood in England.

She married Francis Telfer on 4 May 1839 — just four months after the death of his first wife Jean Murray. The marriage took place in Adelaide, South Australia. Dinah was 18 years old; Francis was 30 with three young children from his first marriage.

Dinah gave birth to a daughter, Jean, on 7 August 1840 at Chain of Ponds in the Adelaide Hills. She died just over three years later, on 20 March 1844 at Chain of Ponds, barely 22 years old. She was buried at West Terrace Cemetery, Adelaide.

Her brief life was marked by the frontier conditions of early South Australia — a young English immigrant who married a widowed Scottish farmer with young children, had a daughter, and died before reaching age 23.

## Timeline

| Date | Event |
|------|-------|
| 10 Jun 1821 | Born — Pytchley, Northamptonshire, England |
| ~1838 | Emigrated to South Australia |
| 4 May 1839 | Married [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]] in Adelaide |
| 7 Aug 1840 | Daughter Jean born at Chain of Ponds, SA |
| 20 Mar 1844 | Died (aged 22) — Chain of Ponds, SA |
| | Buried — West Terrace Cemetery, Adelaide |

## Family Stories

### The Flavel Family Voyage

> *According to Donald Telfer's family history (1986), Chapter 2, pp. 23–24:* Dinah travelled to South Australia aboard the *Prince George* with her parents Joseph and Mary Flavel and her six siblings, alongside the Telfer family. Her brother William Flavel later described walking barefoot from Port Misery through the sandhills, the heat running so painfully between his toes that he "had to run from one bush to another till I got clear of the sand." Dinah married Francis Telfer barely four months after the death of his first wife Jean Murray, becoming stepmother to three young children — James (7), Esther (5), and Elizabeth (4).

## Sources

- **Source:** Donald Telfer, *From the Borders to the Bush* (ISBN 0 7316 6387 X), pp. 21–25 — extract via vision_analyze 19 June 2026
- FindAGrave: [Dinah Flavel Telfer (1821–1844)](https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/166265805) — memorial 166265805, West Terrace Cemetery. Accessed 18 June 2026.
- WikiTree: [Flavel-64](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Flavel-64) — profile for Dinah Flavel. Accessed 18 June 2026.

## Life Summary

Douglas Telfer was the seventh child of John Telfer and Martha Clara Henstridge. Born at Mount Gambier, South Australia on 7 October 1887, he married Lilian Daisy Dawson in 1910. He died in 1956 at Brunswick East, Victoria, suggesting he relocated across the border at some point in his life — possibly for work. His death location in Victoria aligns with several of his siblings who also settled outside South Australia (Colin Roy in NSW, Alan Dale in NSW, Alma Tressy in Victoria).

**⚠️ Death year uncertainty:** The 1956 date is generally accepted in primary family trees. Some records suggest a Douglas Telfer whose ashes were interred at St John's Cemetery, Gordon (New South Wales) on 29 November 1967, while other records point to a Reverend Douglas Telfer operating in Canada. Further verification via NSW BDM registry is needed to confirm whether the 1967 Gordon ashes belong to the Tantanoola Douglas.

## Family Stories

Douglas was born at Mount Gambier in 1887, the seventh child of John Telfer (1840–1913) and Martha Henstridge. He appears in a 1904 wedding party photograph at Koppio Station — a young man seated beside his father James Telfer at the wedding of his sister Agnes Lily to Edwin James Barraud. He later married Lilian Daisy Dawson. *(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.203, 258)*

## Family Stories

Eddie, as he was known, was the seventh child of Francis Charles and Amy Telfer. In June 1987 he wrote a lengthy contribution to the family history, describing his father's journey from Willow Plains to Ungarra in 1906 with horses and wagon, and the back-breaking work of clearing mallee scrub. He recalled family stories with warmth and humour — like the time the family converted a Nash motor car into a horse-drawn buckboard after it broke down, or the gas producer unit fitted to the tractor during the war years that could run on charcoal, allowing them to keep working through fuel shortages. He remembered his father as a great inventor and blacksmith who made a stump-jump plough that worked well in tough conditions. Eddie married twice — first to Lola May Paterson, with whom he had four children including Judith, Miriam, Joy and David, and later to Kayleen Ruth Copping. *(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.136–139)*

# Elizabeth Beattie (1802–1891)

**Role:** Wife of James Telfer (1796–1863) — mother of the South Australian Telfer immigrants
**Born:** 1802 — likely Roxburghshire, Scotland
**Died:** 1891 (aged ~89) — Scotland

## Family

| Relation | Name |
|----------|------|
| **Spouse** | [[James Telfer (1796–1863)]] (m. ~1828) |
| **Son** | [[James Telfer (1829–1914)]] — emigrated to SA |
| **Daughter** | [[Elizabeth Beattie Telfer (1832–1896)]] — m. John Charles Dillon |
| **Son** | [[Robert Telfer (1837–1907)]] — emigrated to SA |
| **Son** | [[John Telfer (1840–1913)]] — emigrated to SA |
| **Son** | [[Adam Francis Telfer (1842–1925)]] — emigrated to SA |

---

## Family Stories

### The Mother Who Stayed Behind

Elizabeth Beattie was born in 1802 and married James Telfer, the eldest son of James Telfer (1761–1845) and Betty Hutton. The couple settled in the Jedburgh area of Roxburghshire, Scotland, where they raised their family. James worked as a farm labourer — a hard life in the Scottish Borders.

### Raising a Family

Elizabeth and James had at least five children who survived to adulthood: James (born 1829), twin daughters Elizabeth and Margaret (1832), Robert (1837), John (1840), and Adam Francis (1842). The 1841 Census shows the family living at Castleton, with James working the land and Elizabeth managing the household.

### Tragedy and Change

In 1863, James Telfer died from injuries sustained in an agricultural accident. This left Elizabeth a widow in her sixties with most of her children grown. The loss of her husband changed everything. One by one, her children made the decision to leave Scotland and seek a new life in South Australia.

James Jr arrived first, followed by Robert, John, and Adam Francis. Even her daughter Elizabeth, now married to John Charles Dillon, made the journey. Elizabeth Beattie stayed behind — the old country was all she knew, and at her age, the voyage was too much. She lived out her remaining years in Scotland, likely with family who remained, passing away in 1891 at around 89 years of age. She never saw her children or grandchildren in Australia again.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.19–20)*

## Sources

- *From the Borders to the Bush* by Hope Simmons (1989), pp.19–20
- 1841 Census, Castleton, Roxburghshire, Scotland
- Statutory Death Index — James Telfer (1863), agricultural accident
- Castleton Parish Records — baptism records

## Life Summary

Elizabeth Beattie Telfer, known as "Betty" in the family, was the second child and eldest daughter of James and Elizabeth Telfer. She was the first of the four siblings to leave Scotland, emigrating to South Australia before her brothers James and Robert. She married John Charles Dillon in 1864.

## Family Stories

Elizabeth Beattie Telfer — known in the family as Betty — was born in 1832 at Castleton in Scotland. She was the only daughter among the five children of James and Elizabeth, and she was the first of them to leave Scotland. She came to South Australia at some point before 1854, settling with their Uncle Francis Telfer at "Macoota" in the Adelaide Hills. She was already here when her brothers James and Robert arrived on the "Oliver Lang" in 1854.

Betty married John Charles Dillon in 1864 at the Mount Gambier area. John had come from Ireland. They made their home in the South East of South Australia and had a large family of ten children — five sons and five daughters — though tragically, one son was stillborn and twin girls lived only 15 minutes.

The Dillon family spread through the South East region. The connection between the Telfers and Dillons runs deep — Betty was the bridge between the two families, and her descendants are still found in the Mount Gambier district today.

Betty died in 1896, aged 64. John Charles Dillon died in 1906 at the age of 79.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp. 214–215)*

## Sources

- **Source:** Donald Telfer, *From the Borders to the Bush* (ISBN 0 7316 6387 X), pp. 33

# Elizabeth Hannah Telfer (1836–1916)

**Role:** Second daughter of Francis Telfer — matriarch of the Farrow line at Hope Farm, Tarlee
**Born:** 7 June 1836 — Dumfriesshire, Scotland
**Died:** 8 October 1916 (aged 80) — Tarlee, South Australia
**Buried:** Tarlee Cemetery (beside husband)
**Spouse:** Charles Farrow (~1836 – Dec 1884) — m. 28 March 1856
**Ship:** *Prince George* — arrived Port Adelaide 26 December 1838 (aged 2)

## Family

| Relation | Name |
|----------|------|
| **Father** | [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]] |
| **Mother** | Jean Murray (1810–1839) |
|| **Husband** | Charles Farrow (~1836 – Dec 1884) ||
| **Sister** | [[Esther Jane Telfer (1834–1909)]] |

### Children (all born at Hope Farm, Tarlee)

| Child | Spouse |
|-------|--------|
| Jane Murray Farrow | Alfred Stribling |
| Esther "Ettie" Farrow | Richard Pelling Latter |
| Elizabeth Telfer Farrow | Thomas Holloway |
| Joseph Francis Farrow | Annie Louise Downton |
| Charles Farrow Jr | Ethel Mary Sambell |
| Amy Farrow | Sidney Stribling |
| John James Telfer Farrow | Emily Smithers |
| George Hope Farrow | Caroline Stanton |
| Mary Bayes Farrow | Alfred Edward Lillecrapp |
| Eva Agnes Farrow | Walter Hookings |

## Life Summary

Elizabeth was born in Dumfriesshire, Scotland to Francis Telfer and Jean Murray. She was just two years old when the family sailed for South Australia on the *Prince George*, arriving at Port Adelaide on 26 December 1838. Her mother Jean died at the Emigration Depot barely a month later.

She grew up at Chain of Ponds and Kersbrook in the Adelaide Hills. On 28 March 1856, aged 19, she married **Charles Farrow** at her family's home on Section 6146, Parra Wirra. The ceremony was performed by Rev. William Vercoe, witnessed by A.B. Murray and P.M. Murray — Elizabeth's uncles.

They settled at **Hope Farm**, Finniss Point, near Tarlee — 152 acres Charles had bought from John Ridley for £319/4. Charles had walked from Kersbrook to Tarlee weekly carrying food, then built a small stone cottage by hand with an axe.

Elizabeth was described as a "very kind and most gracious lady, always quick to help anyone in need." She was a foundation member of Tarlee Baptist Church. After Charles died of pneumonia in 1884, she ran the farm with her sons for over three decades.

Her father Francis Telfer came to stay with Elizabeth at Hope Farm before his death on 2 September 1895, and was buried at Tarlee Cemetery.

She died on 8 October 1916, aged 80, and was buried beside Charles.

## Family Stories

### The Bull at Tuppeny Well

Not long after Charles bought Hope Farm, he was walking there on a hot Monday. About two miles south of Tarlee on the eastern side of the main road was a shallow well called "Tuppeny Well" — the owner charged tuppence to water bullocks and horses. An irate bull came up for a drink. There were no trees nearby, so Charles climbed a six-to-seven-foot whip post used to draw water and sat there until dark when the bull wandered off. Then he walked the remaining six miles home.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, p.59)*

### The Fire of 1865

On Saturday, 25 March 1865, fire destroyed the Farrow cottage. The roof was gone, part of the front wall collapsed, and most of their belongings. Amos Flavel's diary recorded it: *"Mr Farrow helping put out the fire but the roof was destroyed & part of the front wall of the house & a very great deal of other things."*

Charles rebuilt — a larger house with a galvanized iron roof and guttering. It was still standing when the Tarlee reunion was held on 2 December 1984.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.59–60; Amos Flavel Diary, 25 Mar 1865)*

### The Water Walk

During a long dry summer, the rainwater tanks at Hope Farm ran dry. With three small girls to care for, Elizabeth would tie baby Elizabeth Telfer Farrow to the kitchen table leg with a leather strap, take Jane (age 5) and Esther (age 3), and walk 14 miles to Deep Creek to carry back water for the family's daily washing.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, p.61)*

### Charles's Last Night

On 2 December 1884, Charles returned home from his rounds travelling the district with his draught stallion for mating. He was wet through from heavy showers. He told his son Charles Junior to put the horses away: *"I am feeling very ill."*

That night he became much worse. Elizabeth woke Charles Junior to ride to Kapunda for the doctor. The doctor arrived around 4am and promised to return that afternoon. Charles Farrow died just before the doctor got back — pneumonia, in the days before penicillin.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, p.62)*

### Tarlee Baptist Church

In June 1868, the Farrow home hosted the founding meeting of Tarlee Baptist Church. Charles was appointed Deacon and lay preacher, serving for over 16 years. The Minute Book recorded after his death:

> *"This Church deeply mourns the death of Brother Farrow Senior and desires to record the Church's appreciation of his devoted labours in the cause of Christ among us."*

*(From the Borders to the Bush, p.63)*

### Ashley Cooper's 80th Birthday

Ashley Cooper, born in 1908, was the grandson of Elizabeth's daughter Esther Farrow. He worked for the Adelaide Steamship Company as an auditor, travelled to coastal shipping centres, and during WWII was transferred to Perth to oversee merchant ships used as troop carriers. He travelled extensively in the Flinders Ranges — Parachilna, Beltana, Moralana — and wrote a book on the history of Beltana. He suffered a stroke but kept typing one-fingered. He celebrated his 80th birthday in March 1988.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, p.68)*

## Sources

## Life Summary

Elizabeth "Betty" Hutton was born in 1774 and married James Telfer around 1795 in the Castleton / Liddesdale area of the Scottish Borders. She and James raised at least eight children at the family farm in Castleton parish, Roxburghshire.

Her maiden surname is confirmed by the Scottish Statutory Death Index registrations for her children — William Telfer's death entry records mother's maiden surname as "Hutton". This same surname appears in the WikiTree profile for her son Francis Telfer (Telfer-400), linking her as the mother of the Australian immigrant branch.

Betty outlived her husband by eight years. She died in April 1853 and was buried alongside James at Old Castleton Cemetery in Newcastleton.

> **Source:** [FindAGrave — Elizabeth "Betty" Hutton Telfer](https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/170769934/elizabeth_betty-telfer) — accessed 27 May 2026

---

## Family Stories

### The Woman at the Heart of the Clan

Elizabeth "Betty" Hutton was born in 1774 in the Scottish Borders and married James Telfer sometime around 1795. She would go on to be the mother of eight children — five sons and three daughters — and the matriarch of a family that spread from the Liddesdale valley to the other side of the world.

### Life at Greenholm

Betty and James began their married life at Greenholm, a small farming area in Liddesdale near Newcastleton, Roxburghshire. There she gave birth to their first six children between 1796 and 1805: James, Isobel, Adam, Margaret, Robert, and John. Life for a hand-loom weaver's wife was demanding. The cottage was small, the winters were harsh, and there were always hungry mouths to feed. Betty managed her household, raised the children, and kept the family running while James worked the loom and tended the sheep.

### The Move to Blackburnfoot

Sometime around 1805, the family moved a short distance north to a place called Blackburnfoot at the northern end of Newcastleton. The area had its own small weaving industry, which suited James's trade. It was there that Betty's last two children were born — Francis in February 1809, and William in April 1811. Blackburnfoot has since vanished — demolished when the railway line was built through Liddesdale in the 1840s — but it held the childhood home of the man who would one day cross the world.

### The Widow's Years

James Telfer died in December 1845 at the age of 84, leaving Betty a widow after about 50 years of marriage. She outlived him by eight years, dying at Castleton on 14 April 1853 at the age of 79. She was laid to rest beside him in Old Castleton Cemetery. Their headstone reads simply: *"Elizabeth Hutton his spouse"* — a quiet marker for a woman who raised eight children through the hard Border winters, who watched most of them scatter, and whose son Francis would help build a new Telfer legacy in South Australia.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.17–20)*

## Family Stories

### A Quiet Life in Liddesdale

Elizabeth Oliver was born around 1807 and married Robert Telfer, one of the younger brothers of Francis Telfer who would later emigrate to South Australia. Unlike Francis, Robert and Elizabeth stayed in Scotland, living in Newcastleton in the Liddesdale valley where the Telfers had been for generations.

### The 1841 Census Snapshot

The 1841 Census for Newcastleton gives us a rare clear window into Elizabeth's life. The entry reads: "Robert Telfer 36, and Betty 34 with children, Elizabeth 7, James 5, Jean 3, and John 2, also James aged 75, and Betty Hutton 65 of Newcastleton."

So in 1841, Elizabeth (recorded as "Betty") was living with Robert at age 34, with four young children under eight. Also in the household were Robert's elderly parents — James Telfer (75) and Betty Hutton (65) — making it a multi-generational home. This tells us that Elizabeth not only raised her own children but likely helped care for her aging in-laws as well.

### A Short Life

Elizabeth died in 1846 at around 39 years old, leaving Robert a widower with four children to raise — the oldest just twelve. She never lived to see the next chapter of the Telfer story, when some of the next generation would follow Uncle Francis to Australia. Her children — Elizabeth, James, Jean, and John — carried on the family name in Scotland, and some of their descendants would later make the journey to the new world.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, p.18)*

## Sources

- 1841 Census, Newcastleton, Roxburghshire — records Robert Telfer (36), Elizabeth/Betty (34), and children Elizabeth (7), James (5), Jean (3), John (2), plus parents James Telfer (75) and Betty Hutton (65)
- *From the Borders to the Bush* by Hope Simmons (1989), p.18
- Castleton Parish Records, OPR 784/1 — baptism records for Telfer children

body_markdown:
# Esther Jane Telfer (1834–1909)

**Role:** Daughter of Francis Telfer — matriarch of the Smith line
**Born:** 21 May 1834 — Isle of Skye, Scotland
**Died:** March 1909 (aged 75) — Nyngan, New South Wales
**Buried:** Nyngan Cemetery (Church of England section)
**Spouse:** John Smith (~1827 – 5 May 1895)
**Ship:** *Prince George* — arrived Port Adelaide 26 December 1838 (aged 4)

## Family

| Relation | Name |
|----------|------|
| **Father** | [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]] |
| **Mother** | Jean Murray (1810–1839) |
| **Husband** | John Smith |

### Children

| Child | Born | Died | Married |
|-------|------|------|---------|
| Jane Sophie Smith | South Australia | Apr 1913 (aged 47) | Benjamin Harper |
| Margaret Dougal Smith | Burra, S.A. | 30 Oct 1961 (aged ~93) | Thomas Parkins |
| Esther Telfer Smith | 27 Sep 1870, Tungkillo S.A. | 5 May 1896 (aged 25) | Thomas Henry Kent |
| John James "Jack" Smith | 1871, Tungkillo S.A. | — | Idona Caston Murray |
| Francis Telfer "Frank" Smith | 14 Feb 1874, Mt Gambier S.A. | 9 Jul 1945, Nyngan | Ellie Forbes, Catherine Gibson |
| Elizabeth Anne Smith | 1878, Millicent S.A. | — | — |

## Life Summary

### Early Life

Esther was born on the Isle of Skye to Francis Telfer and Jean Murray — the second of their three children. When she was four, the family sailed for South Australia aboard the *Prince George*, arriving at Port Adelaide on 26 December 1838. Her mother Jean died at the Emigration Depot barely a month after landing.

Esther grew up at Chain of Ponds in the Adelaide Hills, then Kersbrook, where her father Francis farmed and helped establish the Church of Christ.

### Marriage to John Smith

On **16 November 1863** at the **Wesleyan Parsonage, Kapunda**, Esther married **John Smith** — a man born in Copenhagen, Denmark in 1830, son of a Scottish Sea Captain and a Danish mother. John had bought a block of land on Gunningbah Creek, north of Nyngan, running sheep. Together they had six children.

### The Move to Victoria

The family set out for Victoria, but Esther, pregnant with her sixth child, found the journey by horse-drawn wagon with steel-rimmed wheels on dirt roads too much. She stayed in Millicent (South East) until after Elizabeth Anne was born in 1878, while John and some of the children pushed on to Natimuk, Victoria to set up a new home.

Their new home, called **"Ebenezer"**, was a pug-and-thatch construction at Sherwood Dam near Mount Arapiles. The children attended Arapiles School.

### The Trek to Nyngan

Towards the end of the 1880s, the two oldest boys — John James and Francis Telfer — rode pushbikes some 600 miles into the outback to Nyngan to scout land. They came back with glowing reports.

The family sold their Natimuk farm to the Lange family and set out on a weeks-long trek to Nyngan in a wagon drawn by four draught horses. Their diet: damper cooked in camp ovens, corned meat, and whatever rabbits and birds they caught along the way. Water bags hung from the side of the wagon in the shade to keep cool.

John bought the block on Gunningbah Creek and ran sheep there until his death on 5 May 1895.

### Later Life

After John died, Esther moved into Nyngan township — a brick home in Wambiana Street. She was described as a tiny person, just five feet tall, a devoted mother and grandmother, and a loyal church supporter.

Her home was still standing in good condition as of 1984.

She died in March 1909, aged 75, and was buried with her husband in Nyngan Cemetery.

## Family Stories

### The Bike Scouts

In the late 1880s, Esther's two boys — John James (about 17) and Francis Telfer (about 15) — rode pushbikes nearly 600 miles from Natimuk, Victoria into the wilds of outback New South Wales to scout land. They returned full of talk about Nyngan and the land opening up. It was their report that convinced the family to pull up roots and make the long trek north.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.39–40)*

### Essie Ray — Esther's Granddaughter

Essie (Esther Jane Harper, granddaughter through Jane Sophie) grew up walking 2.5 miles to school, milking a cow before she left. At about age 11, her family moved from Miram, Victoria to Mullengudgery, NSW. Her mother died of pneumonia about three years later. At just 14, she kept house for six children in a big house with board floors she scrubbed weekly on hands and knees, made butter, did all the cooking, and looked after the lot.

Her brother rode a bike 27 miles into Nyngan to get the doctor — there were no telephones. Too late.

She later married Alex Stevenson (a "nice chap"), had two children. Alex died in his 30th year. She supported herself by dressmaking. Married second to Robert Ray, a widower with two grown daughters. Learned to drive a truck to take fruit from their orchard to the railway.

She celebrated her 90th birthday on 4 January 1989 and still attended Presbyterian Church and Guild, and had a life membership badge from the Orange Show.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.40–41)*

### The Promise to a Dying Sister

Esther's namesake daughter, Esther Telfer Smith, married a Wesleyan minister named Thomas Henry Kent. Thomas died of consumption on 17 December 1895 — just eight months after their wedding. The younger Esther followed him to the grave five months later, also from consumption, on 5 May 1896.

On her deathbed, she asked her sister Margaret: *"If you ever go to Melbourne, will you visit Thomas's grave?"*

Forty-six years later, Margaret — then a widow herself — visited her daughter Ruby and son-in-law Roy Pearce at Bendigo. Roy drove her to Melbourne, and she fulfilled her sister's dying wish.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.44–45)*

### The Eudora Merino Stud

Esther's youngest son, Francis Telfer Smith, drew a block at Mullengudgery (27 miles out of Nyngan) in 1898 and named it **"Eudora"**. He built a large weatherboard home surrounded by shade trees, a big garden with stone fruits and citrus, and a tennis court. He established the Eudora Merino Stud and took sheep to the Royal Sydney Show.

He was a keen pushbike rider in his youth — once rode from Eudora all the way to Mount Gambier with two friends. He also owned racehorses: "Pearl George" and "Pharalie" were sold and shipped to India during WWI.

His daughter Ena recalled: no refrigeration — a charcoal safe with a troublesome door and a green frog living in the water tray on top. Canvas water bags hanging on the verandah. Round galvanised tubs for bathing — knees under chin or legs over the side. Their first car was a T Model Ford; summer nights with the hood down, chugging along at about 20 mph.

When the 1955 flood hit the Bogon River, the Dubbo Aero Club dropped food parcels that burst hitting the water. The family fished tins out of two feet of floodwater — labels lost. They opened cat food for lunch once without realising.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.47–57)*

### Jack Smith Saves Melrose

Esther's oldest son John James "Jack" Smith lived at "Brooklands" on Duck Creek and ran a Merino stud. When his sister Margaret Parkins' husband Thomas was killed in a sulky accident in 1917, Margaret struggled to keep their property "Melrose" going. Her son Dougal hit bad seasons and couldn't make ends meet. The bank threatened to foreclose.

Jack walked into the bank, threw his cheque book on the manager's desk, and said: *"Take what you want out of that, but don't you dare put Margaret Parkins — a widow — out of Melrose."*

Melrose stayed in the Parkins family for 61 years.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.44, 46)*

## Life Summary

Francis Charles Telfer — known as "Charlie" — was born at Kersbrook in the Adelaide Hills on 25 November 1875, the eldest son of John Telfer and Caroline Amelia Masters. He grew up in a farming family and later married Amy Ellen Provis on 6 April 1909 at Stokes, South Australia.

Charlie and Amy raised a large family of **ten children** — six boys and four girls — spanning from 1910 to 1933. Their ninth child was [[Murray John Telfer (1924–2009)]] (1924–2009), Mark's grandfather, who later became a grazier on the Eyre Peninsula.

Charlie passed away on 20 March 1954 at Croydon, Adelaide, aged 78, and was buried at Enfield Memorial Park.

## Family Stories

Francis Charles Telfer — known as Charlie — was born at Kersbrook in the Adelaide Hills in 1875, the eldest son of John and Caroline Telfer. As a young man he drove his horses and wagon down from the family home at Willow Plains near Hawker to the Eyre Peninsula, where he took up 2,000 acres of virgin mallee scrub in the Hundred of Stokes (Ungarra). He had to cut his way into the block with an axe, tether his horses and set up camp. The first task was to dig a small dam with a pick and shovel to catch water for his horses, since the creek that flowed through the property was very salty. He later married Amy Ellen Provis, and they raised ten children in a four-roomed wood-and-iron house with clay floors. Charlie cleared the land using a scrub roller — a heavy log maybe a foot or more in diameter and eight to ten feet long, with chains around it hitched to horses — dragged through the scrub to knock it down before burning. He was a skilled blacksmith, making and mending nearly everything on the farm himself, including an improved stump-jump plough adapted to the tough mallee roots. By 1917 the family was established enough that Charlie could take on the soldiers' block next door when its original owner abandoned it during WWI. His son Edwin Roy remembered him as a great planner, working from daylight until dark, and a man who never let anyone leave his table hungry. *(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.130, 136–138)*

## Family Stories

### The Name That Continued

Francis Telfer was born around 1768 at Sorbietrees, Roxburghshire, the second son of James Telfer of Sorbietrees and Margaret Armstrong. His life is one of the pieces we can't fully recover — we know he was baptised, we know when he died, and his name is carved on the family headstone in Castleton Cemetery alongside his parents and siblings.

But that name carried weight. "Francis" appears regularly in succeeding generations — his nephew Francis Telfer (1809–1895) made the voyage to South Australia, and his great-grandnephew Francis Charles Telfer (1875–1954) carried it across the ocean. The stone is the record; the descendants are the story.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.17-19)*

# Francis Telfer (1809–1895)

**Role:** Immigrant progenitor — founded the Australian Telfer branch. Arrived SA 1838
**Born:** 2 February 1809 — Blackburn Foot (Black Burn fort), Liddesdale, Roxburghshire, Scotland
**Died:** 2 September 1895 (aged 86) — Hope Farm, Tarlee, South Australia
**Buried:** Tarlee Cemetery, Tarlee, District Council of Clare and Gilbert Valleys, South Australia
**Occupation:** Farmer — Hope Farm, Tarlee
**Ship:** *Prince George* (482 tons, 118 ft, 3-masted, Captain Young) — arrived Port Adelaide 26 December 1838

## Life Summary

Francis Telfer was born on 2 February 1809 at Blackburn Foot (the old Black Burn fort) in Liddesdale, Roxburghshire, Scotland — the seventh of eight children born to James Telfer and Elizabeth "Betty" Hutton. He grew up in the Castleton region of the Scottish Borders.

### The Voyage

Francis emigrated to South Australia aboard the *Prince George*, departing London in September 1838 and arriving at Port Adelaide on 26 December 1838. He travelled with his first wife Jean Murray and their three young children: James (6), Esther (4), and Elizabeth (2). A fourth child, John (the baby), died during the voyage.

### Three Marriages

Francis outlived his first two wives. Jean Murray died shortly after arrival at the Emigration Depot in Adelaide on 22 January 1839 — barely a month after landing. Her infant son John had died during the voyage.

Within months, Francis married **Dinah Flavel** (a young English immigrant from Northamptonshire) on 4 May 1839. They had one daughter, Jean (born at Chain of Ponds, 1840). Dinah died on 20 March 1844 at Chain of Ponds, aged only 22, and was buried at West Terrace Cemetery, Adelaide.

On 27 March 1845, Francis married **Margaret Wright**, with whom he had three more children: John (the main line ancestor), Margaret Dougal, and George Wright. Margaret Wright brought stability to the household and outlived Francis, dying in 1892.

### Later Life

Francis farmed at Chain of Ponds and Kersbrook in the Adelaide Hills before settling at **Hope Farm, Tarlee**, in the Clare Valley region. He became a respected local identity. By the time of his death at age 86, he had established the Telfer name across South Australia.

His obituary in *The Border Watch* (18 September 1895) recorded:
> "He leaves two sons — Mr. John Telfer, of Hawker, and Mr. G. W. Telfer, Willaston — and three daughters — Mrs. Farrow, of Hope Farm, Mrs. Smith, of Canouba, New South Wales, and Mrs. A. F. Telfer, of Edgerston, Tantanoola."

Francis died at Hope Farm, Tarlee on 2 September 1895. A memorial headstone was erected by the Telfer Family History Association in 1999, commemorating his three wives and his place as the founder of the Australian Telfer line.

## Family Stories

### The Lost Boy — James Telfer (1832–1845)

Francis's eldest son James, aged 13, disappeared while bringing in stray sheep during heavy rain in July 1844 near Chain of Ponds. Neighbours, police — they scoured the flooded countryside for days. Nothing. The *South Australian Register* ran a notice on 10 Jul 1844 asking for information. James was never seen alive again.

Around 1877, floodwaters receded near Adelaide and a human skeleton was found lodged against a tree in the river. A doctor said it was a boy about 13, probably there 20+ years. Whether Francis ever found out is unknown.

It was the fourth family member Francis lost in six years: infant John (died at sea, 1838), wife Jean (1839), wife Dinah (1844), and his eldest son James.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.25–27; SA Register, 10 Jul 1844)*

### The Flavel Family and the Voyage of the *Prince George*

Francis sailed to South Australia on the *Prince George* alongside the Flavel family — Joseph and Mary Flavel and their seven kids. The Flavels became lifelong friends. William Flavel remembered arriving at Port Misery on 26 Dec 1838 and walking barefoot across the sandhills, where the summer sand was so hot he "had to run from one bush to another till I got clear of the sand." The Flavel baby, John Telfer, died during the voyage and was buried at sea.

The *Prince George* was a 482-ton, 118-foot, 3-masted barque under Captain Young. Francis applied for emigration on 9 August 1838, had just 26 days to prepare, and sailed from London on 4 September 1838.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.22–24)*

### Francis and the Kersbrook Church of Christ

Francis was an intensely religious man. He regularly walked 22 miles from Kersbrook to Adelaide for the "Scotch Kirk" (Gouger Street United Presbyterian Church). In 1863, he became a founding trustee of the Kersbrook Church of Christ Chapel and served as Sunday School Superintendent. He was described as "the pastor's right hand" alongside John McMillan.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.27–31)*

### Francis's Last Letter — To Jane Murray Perry

About a month before Francis died at age 86, he wrote a letter to his granddaughter Jane Murray Perry (the daughter of his daughter Jean/Jane Telfer). The letter was written at Hope Farm, Tarlee and spoke of his life, his belief in God, and his hopes for his family. It is one of the few surviving documents in Francis's own hand — a direct connection to the man who founded the Australian Telfer line.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, p.33)*

### The House at Macoota

Francis's stone house at Section 6146, Kersbrook had walls 15 inches thick of local stone. Originally shingle-roofed (still preserved under later iron), it had a central passage, three bedrooms off the south side, a kitchen/dining room and drawing room with large fireplaces on the north, and a well about 50 yards from the back door. The land was so thick with wattle and banksia scrub you couldn't walk through it when first taken up.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.31–33)*

### Margaret Wright and the Stirling Castle Legend

Family legend had it that Francis's third wife Margaret Wright was "born in Stirling Castle" — though which bit of the castle was left for debate. Problem is, the last king to actually live there was James VI (1567–1625), long before Margaret was born. Colourful story, suspect geography.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, p.27)*

# Frederick Parker (~1838–1928)

**Role:** Second husband of Jean Telfer
**Died:** 1928 — Wildes Meadow, New South Wales
**Buried:** Bowral Cemetery, NSW

Frederick Parker, son of George Parker, married Jean (who had by then adopted the name Jane) on Christmas Day 1871 at Kapunda. They lived at Finniss Point before moving to the far north of South Australia around Hawker and Oraparinna.

After Jane died in 1892 from heart disease, Frederick later went to live with his elder daughter Margaret and son-in-law Edward Liebich at Wildes Meadow, New South Wales. He died in 1928 and is buried in Bowral Cemetery.

**Source:** *From the Borders to the Bush* — Chapter on Jean/Jane Telfer

## Family Stories

After Jean Telfer, by then known as Jane, lost her first husband Richard Paynter to pleurisy in 1869, she remarried on Christmas Day 1871. Her new husband was Frederick Parker, described in the book as an itinerant farm labourer and bullock driver, son of George Parker. They were married at the Wesleyan Church in Kapunda, with Jane's brother-in-law Charles Farrow and niece Jane Farrow as witnesses. The family left Finniss Point and moved to the far north of South Australia, living around Hawker and Oraparinna. Their children — Margaret Eliza, Frederick George, Annie, Martha, Joanna Wittita Cordley, and Ethel May — were born at various places across that remote country. Frederick is believed to have worked as a railway ganger at Finniss during the later years. Jane died of heart disease on 15 July 1892 at Queens Own Town and was buried at Strathalbyn Cemetery. After many years, Frederick went to live with his eldest daughter Margaret and her husband Edward Liebich at Wildes Meadow, New South Wales. He died in Berrima Hospital on 12 August 1928 and is buried in Bowral Cemetery. At the time of his death, only three of his children — Margaret, Frederick (known as George), and Joanna — survived him.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, p.93)*

body_markdown:
# George Wright Telfer (1850–1913)

**Role:** Youngest child of Francis Telfer and Margaret Wright — the one who went west

**Born:** 22 November 1850 — Macoota, Kersbrook, South Australia
**Died:** 1913 — Nungarin, Western Australia
**Occupation:** Farmer, grocer, butter maker, steam laundry proprietor
**Spouse:** Ruth Penna (m. 17 Sept 1884, d. 1908)

---

## Family

| Relation | Name |
|----------|------|
| **Mother** | [[Margaret Wright Telfer (?–1892)]] |
| **Father** | [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]] |
| **Spouse** | Ruth Penna (m. 17 Sep 1884) |
| **Children** | William Francis Telfer (1885–1955), Olive Millie Telfer (1890–1890), Lesley Thomas Telfer (1892–1914), Olive Netta Telfer (1894–1986) |
| **Siblings** | [[John Telfer (1847–1929)]], [[Margaret Dougal Telfer (1849–1936)]] |

---

## Family Stories

### The Youngest Son

George Wright was the baby of the family — born at Macoota, Kersbrook on 22nd November 1850, the youngest son of Francis and Margaret. He grew up working his father's farm alongside brother John, learning the market gardening trade from the ground up. When he was old enough, he bought land of his own in the Kersbrook area and built himself a home. He wasn't one to stay in someone else's shadow. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.180)*

### The Grocer Who Went the Distance

Long before road trains and highways, George ran a grocery van all the way to Port Augusta. That's a hell of a trip from Kersbrook — hundreds of miles of rough track, dirt roads, and outback settlements. He'd load up his van with supplies and make the journey north, peddling his goods to the scattered communities along the way. It was the kind of work that built character, or at least a strong back. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.180)*

### The Land Speculator

George had an eye for a deal. He wasn't content with just farming — he bought and sold land like a man who could see which way the wind was blowing. He picked up blocks at Kensington that had once belonged to his mother, took out a mining lease at Kadina, and bought several sections at Hawker which he later sold to his brother John. He was always looking for the next opportunity, never one to sit still. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.180)*

### Ruth Penna of Kersbrook

On 17th September 1884, at the age of 33, George married Ruth Penna. She was 21, the daughter of William and Ruth Penna, also market gardeners from Kersbrook. The wedding was in her parents' home, solemnized by the Rev. John Hall, Presbyterian minister. Ruth must have known what she was signing up for — life with George was never going to be quiet. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.180)*

### The Salem Baptist Years

In December 1885, George and Ruth were welcomed into the fellowship of Salem Baptist Church at Gumeracha. George wasn't just a pew-warmer either — he was soon elected secretary of the church. This was the same faith that ran through the whole Telfer family, that same Baptist thread that had followed them from Scotland through Kersbrook and beyond. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.180)*

### Three Children, Two Continents

While they were at Kersbrook, Ruth gave George three children: William Francis in August 1885, Olive Millie in March 1890, and Lesley Thomas in 1892. Little Olive only lived about two months — she was buried in the Gawler Cemetery on 5th May 1890, her parents' address listed as Mount Pleasant. It was a hard loss, the kind that marked a family. But life pushed on, and George kept moving. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.180)*

### Father Francis Comes to Stay

After Margaret Wright died in 1892, old Francis came to live with George and Ruth. He was getting on by then, his health fading. In 1893 they all packed up and moved to Willaston, near Gawler, where George turned his hand to running a butter factory. It was a complete change from market gardening — but that was George, always ready to try something new. A year later, in June 1894, Ruth gave birth to another daughter, Olive Netta. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.180)*

### The Westward Gamble

Some time in 1896, George made the biggest decision of his life. He packed up Ruth, the children, and the remnants of the household and moved the whole family to Western Australia. They lived in Albany for a few years first, then moved to Perth where they ran a boarding house overlooking the Swan River. From market gardener to butter maker to boarding house proprietor — George wasn't afraid to reinvent himself. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.180)*

### The City Steam Laundry

From boarding house to laundry — George established the City Steam Laundry in Leederville, and by 1901 he was listed as manager. By 1902-03 it was "Telfer & Penna, proprietors," with his brother-in-law Thomas Penna as partner. Their ads boasted "Special quotations for Hotels" and a telephone number — number 464, which was something in those days. In 1908 they opened a branch on Hay Street in Perth, and the name changed to City Steam Laundry & Dye Works. The place was still operating as the Monarch Laundry as late as 1981, long after George was gone. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.180)*

### The Loss of Ruth

1908 was a hard year. Ruth died, leaving George with three children to raise and a business to run. The laundry was split — son Frank took over Telfer's City Steam Laundry with two Hay Street branches, while George kept Telfer's Cleaning & Dye Works at Newcastle Street, Leederville. He pushed on, but something must have gone out of him with Ruth. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.180-181)*

### The Merredin Years

Around 1912, George sold the laundry business and moved east along the railway line to Merredin. He opened a store there and bought a farming property at nearby Nungarin. He and his sons ran both for a year or so — a final attempt to build something in this new country. But George died in 1913, not long after they'd settled. The following year his younger son Lesley Thomas was killed in an accident on the same farm. Within two years, George and both his sons were gone from the land he'd tried so hard to work. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.181)*

---

## Life Story

George Wright Telfer was the youngest child of Francis Telfer (1809–1895) and his third wife, Margaret Wright. He was born at Macoota, Kersbrook on 22nd November 1850.

He spent his early years working his father's farm at Kersbrook, then bought land of his own and built a home. He ran a grocery van to Port Augusta, speculated in land across Kensington, Kadina, and Hawker, and married Ruth Penna in 1884.

After his mother's death in 1892, his father Francis came to live with them, and in 1893 the family moved to Willaston where George ran a butter factory. In 1896 he moved the entire family to Western Australia — first Albany, then Perth, where he ran a boarding house before establishing the City Steam Laundry in Leederville.

After Ruth's death in 1908, George carried on the business, then sold up around 1912 and moved to Merredin where he opened a store and bought a farm at Nungarin. He died in 1913. His son Lesley was killed in an accident the following year.

**Source:** *From the Borders to the Bush* — pages 30, 180-181

Gilbert Melville Telfer (the book records his given names as Gilbert Melville, not Melvin McLeod — he was known as "Mel") was born in 1911, the third child of Mark Telfer (1877–1946) and Julia Matilda Seebohm (1876–1939) of Tantanoola, South Australia.

He married Jessie Allan and they had three children — Beth, who married Clive Lipscombe; Ian, who married Sally Taylor; and Allan, who married Christine Marshall.

Mel was a good footballer, playing at centre wing and proving formidable as a fast player and a good ball handler. He was an opening batsman for the Tantanoola Cricket team and made many centuries. He was a most useful member of the team and excelled as the wicket keeper. When his eyesight no longer permitted him to play football and cricket, Mel played bowls, both indoor and outdoor, and proved to be an excellent player.

Like his father and brothers, he was interested in local affairs and was a Life Member of the Tantanoola Pastoral, Agricultural and Horticultural Society.

In his father's obituary, he was listed as "Mel Telfer, Tantanoola".

## Family Stories

Mel was the third child of Mark and Tillie Telfer. The book describes him as a fine sportsman — a good footballer who played centre wing, fast and a good ball handler; an opening batsman for the Tantanoola Cricket team who made many centuries and excelled as wicket keeper. When his eyesight no longer allowed him to play football and cricket, he took up bowls, both indoor and outdoor, and proved an excellent player. Like his father and brothers, he was interested in local affairs and was a Life Member of the Tantanoola Pastoral, Agricultural and Horticultural Society. He married Jessie Allan and they had three children — Beth, Ian and Allan. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.243)*

## Life Summary

Isabella Lucieton Telfer was the third child of John Telfer and Martha Clara Henstridge. Born at Edgerston, South Australia on 17 July 1880, she married Alexander Brown Thomson on 12 July 1911. She lived to the age of 83, passing on 30 June 1964 at Klemzig, South Australia. Her death place — Klemzig, a north-eastern suburb of Adelaide — suggests she may have moved closer to the city in her later years, possibly to be nearer to family.

**Note:** Her records must be distinguished from other Isabella Thomsons of the same era — an Isabella Thomson who died in Western Australia (Karrakatta) in 1936, and a Scottish Isabella Thomson who died in Polmont in 1935. The 1964 Klemzig death date is the correct match for the Tantanoola Telfer line.

## Family Stories

Isabella Lucieton Telfer was the eighth child of John and Martha Telfer. She married Alexander Thomson, and together they had three children — Roma, Trevor and Murray. Her life, like that of many of her siblings, was rooted in the Tantanoola district where the Telfer family had established themselves after arriving from Scotland.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, p.240)*

body_markdown:
# Isobel Telfer (1798–1875)

**Role:** Sister of Francis Telfer (1809–1895), stayed in Scotland

Isobel Telfer was born on 10 February 1798 at Greenholm, near Newcastleton, Roxburghshire, Scotland. She was the second child of James Telfer (1761–1845), a hand loom weaver, and Elizabeth "Betty" Hutton (1774–1853). Her name is also recorded as "Isabella".

She did NOT emigrate to Australia and died in 1875 in Scotland.

The book states: *"We have no further information about four members of this family; namely Isobel, Adam, Margaret and William."* Like her younger siblings Adam, Margaret, and William, Isobel's fate after the family records is not documented beyond her death.

## Family Stories

### The Sister Who Stayed

Isobel Telfer was born on 10 February 1798 at Greenholm, outside Newcastleton in the Scottish Borders. She was the second child and first daughter of James Telfer and Betty Hutton — the weaver and his wife raising a growing family in a cottage with its own cow.

Her baptism is there in the Old Parish Register for Castleton, clear as day. But after that? Nothing. The book says it plain: *"We have no further information about four members of this family; namely Isobel, Adam, Margaret and William."*

She was 39 when her brother Francis packed up and sailed for South Australia in 1838. She was 47 when her father died in 1845. And she was still in Scotland when her older brother James — the one who emigrated — passed away in 1863. She died in 1875, aged 77, still in Scotland, her life unrecorded.

Some stories are lost because nobody wrote them down. Isobel's is one of them.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.17-20)*

**Source:** *From the Borders to the Bush* — pages 17–20

# James Telfer (1761–1845)

**Role:** Scottish progenitor — father of South Australian immigrant [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]]
**Born:** ~1761 — baptised 14 Jul 1761, Castleton, Roxburghshire, Scotland
**Died:** 19 December 1845 — Castleton, Scottish Borders, Scotland
**Buried:** Old Castleton Cemetery, Newcastleton, Scottish Borders, Scotland
**Spouse:** [[Elizabeth Hutton Telfer (1774–1853)]] (m. ~1795)

## Family

| Relation | Name |
|----------|------|
| **Spouse** | [[Elizabeth Hutton Telfer (1774–1853)]] — Elizabeth "Betty" Hutton (m. ~1795) |

| **Son** | Robert Telfer (bap. 23 Apr 1803, d. 1878) — m. Elizabeth Oliver |
| **Son** | John Telfer (bap. 20 Mar 1805, d. 3 Mar 1839) — unmarried |
| **Son** | [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]] (bap. 2 Feb 1809, d. 1895) — emigrated to SA |
| **Son** | William Telfer (bap. 6 Apr 1811, d. 1881) |
| **Father** | John Telfer (of Castleton) (~1731–?) |
| **Mother** | Elspeth Young (~1722–?) |

## Life Summary

James Telfer was born around 1761 in the Liddesdale/Castleton area of Roxburghshire, Scottish Borders. He was baptised at Castleton on 14 July 1761, the son of John Telfer of Castleton. He married Elizabeth "Betty" Hutton around 1795.

James and Betty raised at least eight children in the Castleton parish, Roxburghshire, near the English-Scottish border. Their son Francis emigrated to South Australia in 1838 aboard the *Prince George*, establishing the Australian Telfer branch.

According to Donald Telfer's *From the Borders to the Bush* (1989), James was known as a hard-working farm man in the Liddesdale region. His descendants in Scotland continued farming the same area.

James died on 19 December 1845 at Castleton and was buried at Old Castleton Cemetery, Newcastleton. His wife Betty outlived him by eight years.

## Timeline

| Date | Event |
|------|-------|
| 14 Jul 1761 | Baptised — Castleton, Roxburghshire, Scotland |
| ~1795 | Married Elizabeth "Betty" Hutton |
| 1796–1811 | Eight children born at Castleton |
| 1838 | Son Francis emigrated to South Australia |
| 19 Dec 1845 | Died — Castleton, Scottish Borders |
| | Buried — Old Castleton Cemetery, Newcastleton |

## Family Stories

### The Greenholm Years

James Telfer didn't start out in Castleton itself. He and Betty lived first at Greenholm, a little farming area in Liddesdale where their first five children were baptised between 1796 and 1805 — James, Isobel, Adam, Margaret, Robert, and John. Life was simple and hard. The Telfers were sheep farmers and hand-loom weavers, like most of their neighbours in the Scottish Borders. They worked their small land holdings with the seasons, shearing and weaving wool to make ends meet.

### The Move to Blackburnfoot

Sometime between 1805 and 1809, James moved the family from Greenholm to Blackburnfoot — another farmstead in the same Liddesdale valley. It was there that their last two sons were born: Francis in February 1809, and William in April 1811. Francis would go on to become the one who crossed the world. But back then he was just another bairn in a packed cottage in the Borders, learning the shepherd's trade from his father.

### A Hand Loom Weaver's Life

In those days the Telfers of Roxburghshire were what the old parish records call "hand loom weavers" — men who worked wool at home on their own looms, spinning and weaving the fleece from the sheep that grazed the Cheviot Hills. It was honest, calloused-hand work that paid just enough to keep a family fed. The Industrial Revolution was already reshaping Scotland, but up in Liddesdale, the old ways held on a little longer. James lived and died in that world, never leaving the valley he was born in.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.17–20)*

## Sources

- **Source:** Donald Telfer, *From the Borders to the Bush* (ISBN 0 7316 6387 X), pp. 17–20 — extract via vision_analyze 18 June 2026
