## Life Summary

James Telfer was born in 1796 at Castleton, Roxburghshire, the eldest of eight children of James Telfer and Elizabeth "Betty" Hutton. He married Elizabeth Beattie around 1825 and stayed in Scotland when his younger brother Francis emigrated to South Australia in 1838.

James and Elizabeth farmed in the Liddesdale/Castleton area, where they raised at least five children. Their descendants continued in the Scottish Borders region.

## Family Stories

James Telfer was the first child of James and Betty Telfer, born at Greenholm in 1796. He married Elizabeth Beattie around 1830 and stayed in Scotland as the eldest brother, while Francis set off for South Australia. Four of James's sons and one daughter would eventually follow their uncle across the world in later years.

Getting reliable records of James and Elizabeth's family has been a challenge. The children — with the exception of the youngest, Adam — were apparently never baptised, which suggests the family attended a non-conformist church during those years. Many births simply weren't registered because of a government tax of one shilling, which was a significant amount of money at the time.

The 1851 Jedburgh Census shows James as a 52-year-old agricultural labourer born in Roxburghshire, living with his wife Betty (48), and their children Ellen (19, servant), Bellie (14, servant), John (13, scholar) and Adam (9, scholar). Also in the household were Robert Beattie, a 77-year-old widower labourer (likely Elizabeth's father), and a nephew also named Robert Beattie, aged 11. James, Robert, Elizabeth and Margaret were already out of the home by then. The same census lists a Robert Telfer, aged 16, agricultural labourer, born Newcastleton, living at Falside Stable — this would have been James and Elizabeth's son Robert.

James Telfer died at 4pm on 9th December, 1863, at his dwelling house at Falside, Southdean, Roxburghshire. The cause was injuries he received from being squeezed between the shafts of a cart and a granary wall. His youngest son Adam reported the death. Elizabeth died on 28th December, 1891, at the age of 89, from "natural decay" — a quiet end after a long life.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp. 188)*

- **Source:** Donald Telfer, *From the Borders to the Bush* (ISBN 0 7316 6387 X), pp. 19–20 — extract via vision_analyze 18 June 2026

## Life Summary

James Telfer was the eldest son of James Telfer and Elizabeth Beattie. Born at the ruins of Hermitage Castle in Liddesdale, he emigrated to South Australia at age 25 on the ship "Oliver Lang", arriving in Melbourne in 1854 with his brother Robert and sister Elizabeth. He went on to manage Koppio Station near Port Lincoln for 39 years and became one of the colony's leading wool experts.

## Family Stories

James Telfer was born on 3rd September, 1829 at Hermitage Castle, Liddesdale, Roxburghshire, Scotland — the eldest son of James Telfer and Elizabeth Beattie. He came to Australia at the age of 25 on the ship "Oliver Lang", in company with his brother Robert and sister Elizabeth.

According to the official shipping list, the "Oliver Lang" departed Liverpool on 25th July, 1854, and arrived in Melbourne on 25th September, 1854. The Master was Henry Manning, tonnage 1736, and the ship carried 445 passengers. James, Robert and Elizabeth were listed as "adults" and "English" — though they were of course Scots — but with so many folks emigrating, officials weren't fussy about accuracy.

After landing in Melbourne, the three made their way to South Australia where they made contact with their Uncle Francis Telfer at Kersbrook in the Adelaide Hills.

James was under contract to Mr. Alexander Borthwick Murray and worked as a shepherd at Tungkillo for five years. While still there, he married Janet Welsh, the daughter of John and Margaret Welsh of Nisbet, Scotland. The marriage took place at "the Manse", Wakefield Street, on 6th November, 1855, according to the rites of the Church of Scotland, conducted by the Rev. Robert Haining. The witnesses were Robert and Elizabeth Telfer — his brother and sister.

After his five years at Tungkillo, James took over the management of Koppio Station near Port Lincoln for Dr. John Harris Browne. He managed Koppio for 39 years and in addition looked after "Talia", "Kalka" and "Pondanna" Stations in the Gawler Ranges. This meant many miles of arduous travel over unmade roads in all weathers.

James was recognised as one of the State's leading experts in wool production. Koppio Station carried 25,000 sheep, and the wool produced there and on the West Coast and Gawler Ranges stations was noted for its very high quality.

James and Janet's family of seven children grew up at Koppio Station. Two gum trees that still stand near the entrance were named "James" and "Janet" after the twins.

Janet died in 1885 after a long illness. James wrote a letter to his son James that described her last hours — it's preserved in the family records. James lived on until about 1914.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp. 189–192)*

## Sources

- **Source:** Donald Telfer, *From the Borders to the Bush* (ISBN 0 7316 6387 X), pp. 22–23

# James Telfer (1832–1845)

**Role:** Eldest son of [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]] and Jean Murray — vanished at age 13

## Family

## Life Summary

James was born in Scotland in 1832, the eldest of Francis and Jean's kids. He made the voyage on the *Prince George* with his parents and two younger sisters, docking at Port Adelaide on 26 December 1838. His mother died just 27 days later — leaving Francis with three kids under 7.

James grew up in the Adelaide Hills frontier on his father's farm near Chain of Ponds. By 13 he was working as a shepherd on the family sheep station.

## Family Stories

### The Disappearance of James Telfer

In July 1844, during a week of heavy rain, James left the sheep station on the River Torrens near Chain of Ponds to round up stray sheep. He never came home.

Francis raised the alarm that night. Neighbours searched for days but the creeks were flooded and rain hadn't let up. Nothing was found. The general feeling was the flood took him. People figured when waters dropped, his remains would turn up in the riverbed or the Reedbeds. They didn't.

The *South Australian Register* printed this on 10 July 1844 (p.3):

> **"BOY MISSING** — On Tuesday last, during the heavy rain then falling, a youth named Telfer, thirteen years old, left his fathers sheep station on the River Torrens, near Chain of Ponds, to recover some stray sheep, but up to Saturday last had not been heard of. The surrounding country has been searched, but no trace of the wanderer has been found: and from the late inclemency of the weather, there is too much reason to believe that he has perished."

Family stories over the years threw up different theories — killed by aborigines, step-mother troubles, ran away. The most detailed version came from William Flavel: one morning someone walked twelve miles to tell Francis, who rounded up every man in the district. They searched for days, then got the police from Adelaide. Nothing.

Then around 1877 — 33 years later — a newspaper article reported that recent floods had washed away logs and debris lodged against a tree in the river near Adelaide. Amongst the debris was a human skeleton. Police took charge. A doctor said the bones were a boy about 13, probably there for more than 20 years.

Whether Francis ever learned his son had been found is unknown.

Tragically, James was the fourth family member Francis had lost in six years — wife Jean (1839), infant son John (died at sea 1838), second wife Dinah (1844), and now his eldest boy.

*(Based on Donald Telfer, From the Borders to the Bush, pp.25–27, and the SA Register, 10 Jul 1844)*

## Sources

- Donald Telfer, *From the Borders to the Bush* (ISBN 0 7316 6387 X), pp. 25–27 — story reference, not verbatim
- South Australian Register, 10 July 1844, Page 3, Col. A — public domain newspaper quote

# James Telfer (1866–1946)

**Born:** 18 Oct 1866, Honeysuckle Flat SA | **Died:** 28 Aug 1946, Glencoe West SA (age 79) | **Mother:** Martha Allen | **Father:** [[John Telfer (1840–1913)]] | **Spouse:** Alma Ida Sporer (1881–1965) (m. 24 Oct 1917) | **Occupation:** Farmer/Newspaper agent

## Family

## Life Summary

James Telfer was the first child and eldest son of [[John Telfer (1840–1913)]] and his first wife [[Martha Allen (1840–1876)]]. Born at Honeysuckle Flat, South Australia on 18 October 1866, James was the first of four children from this marriage and carried his paternal grandfather's name.

In 1895, James—then living at Tantanoola—was listed in the *Border Watch* Almanac as a newspaper agent for the district, suggesting he operated a local agency for the Mount Gambier newspaper. The 1894 Tantanoola Show concert featured him as a performer, and Border Watch advertisements from 1898 and 1900 confirm his newspaper agency at Tantanoola.

He married Alma Ida Sporer (1881–1965) on 24 October 1917 at the Lutheran Church, Mount Gambier — James was 49, Alma was 37. Their only child, Vida, was born on 8 March 1919. James became a prominent community figure in Glencoe West: he was appointed a Justice of the Peace in 1924, served as District Council Auditor (re-elected 1927), and acted as Secretary of the Glencoe District Hall in 1929.

He died on 28 August 1946 at Glencoe West, South Australia, aged 79. His obituary in The Advertiser (2 Sep 1946) and The Chronicle (5 Sep 1946) described him as the beloved husband of Alma and loving father of Vida.

## Family Stories

James was the first of John and Martha Telfer's four children, born at Honeysuckle Flat on 18 October 1866. He moved with the family to Tantanoola as a young boy and quickly became involved in community life. He served as the first Secretary of the Tantanoola Agricultural and Floral Society and was also Secretary of the committee formed to organise the building of a Presbyterian Church in the town.

In 1917 he married Alma Ida Sporer at Mount Gambier, and together they established a general store at Glencoe West that also housed the local Post Office and sold groceries, hardware, drapery and anything else the farming community might need. James was an Elder at the local Presbyterian Church — a quiet, gentle soul who loved reading, especially poetry. He was Patron of the Glencoe West Tennis Club, served as its Auditor, and was an enthusiastic supporter of the Cricket Club. Always ready to lend a hand, James was a pillar of the community until his death in 1946. He and Alma had one daughter, Vida.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.235–236)*

James Telfer Dillon was born in 1861 at Kooringa, South Australia, the eldest son of Elizabeth Beattie Telfer and John Charles Dillon. He was named after his maternal grandfather [[James Telfer (1796–1863)]], following the Scottish naming tradition of passing the surname as a middle name.

**Role:** Fourth child and eldest daughter of Mark Telfer and Julia Seebohm

Jean Maryann Martha Telfer was born in 1910, the fourth child of Mark Telfer (1877–1946) and Julia Matilda Seebohm (1876–1939) of Tantanoola, South Australia. She was the eldest daughter.

Jean was named Maryann Martha after her paternal grandmother [[Martha Henstridge (~1854–1921)]] and her maternal grandmother — a naming tradition that connects her to both sides of the family.

## Family Stories

Jean Maryann Martha Telfer was the fourth child and eldest daughter of Mark Telfer and Julia Matilda Seebohm, born in 1910 at Tantanoola. She never married. For some years she lived and worked at "Pleasant Hill", Glencoe West, the home of her father's cousin, Frank Telfer, and his wife Clara. Jean was a foundation member of the Tantanoola Women's Agricultural Bureau, formed in 1931, and remained active in its work. When her father retired to Millicent, Jean accompanied him, keeping house for him in his later years. She was a highly skilful bowler, both indoor and outdoor. Jean died on 16 September 1984 at the age of 74 and was buried in Tantanoola Cemetery, where her grave is shared with her sister Maifie, the inscription reading: "In Loving Memory of our dear Sisters."

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.244, 250)*

body_markdown:
# Jean Murray (1810–1839)

**Role:** First wife of [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]] — mother of his first three children. Arrived SA 1838.
**Born:** 1810 — Eskdalemuir, Dumfriesshire, Scotland
**Died:** 22 January 1839 — Emigration Depot, Adelaide, South Australia
**Buried:** Adelaide, South Australia

---

## Family Stories

### The Voyage That Took Everything

Jean Murray married Francis Telfer around 1831 in Eskdalemuir, in the Scottish Borders. They had three children — James, Esther and Elizabeth — all born in Scotland and Skye. In September 1838, the young family boarded the *Prince George* in London, bound for South Australia.

The voyage took about 14 weeks. During the journey, Jean gave birth to a fourth child, a boy they named John. The baby didn't survive the voyage.

They arrived at Port Adelaide on 26 December 1838 after a hellish three and a half months at sea. Jean was frail from childbirth and the conditions on board. She never recovered. Just 27 days after stepping onto Australian soil, she died at the Emigration Depot in Adelaide on 22 January 1839. She was about 28 years old.

Francis was left a widower with three children under the age of seven in a new country, with no wife and no family nearby. He eventually remarried Margaret Wright, who became the mother of John Telfer (1847–1929) and the rest of that branch.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.21-22)*

---

## Life Summary

Jean Murray was born in 1810 at Eskdalemuir, Dumfriesshire, Scotland. She married Francis Telfer around 1831 in Scotland and bore three children — James (1832), Esther (1834), and Elizabeth (1836) — all born in the Scottish Borders and Skye regions.

The family emigrated to South Australia aboard the *Prince George*, departing London in September 1838. Jean travelled with Francis and their three young children. A fourth child, John (the baby), was born during the voyage but died at sea.

They arrived at Port Adelaide on 26 December 1838 after a voyage of approximately 14 weeks. Jean died just 27 days later at the Emigration Depot in Adelaide on 22 January 1839 — likely from the combined effects of the arduous voyage and complications from childbirth.

Her death left Francis a widower with three small children under the age of 7.

title: Jean (Jane) Telfer (1840–1892) — Daughter of Francis Telfer
roles: Leased/worked farmland at Arden Vale (near Quorn, SA). Later worked properties around Peterborough.
body_markdown:
# Jean (Jane) Telfer (1840–1892)

Third daughter of **[[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]]** and **Jean Murray**. After her mother's death, she was step-raised by **Dinah Flavel** (her father's second wife).

## Vital Information

- **Born:** 7 August 1840
- **Birth name:** Jean Telfer (marriage certificate gives name as "Jane")
- **Died:** 15 July 1892, Queens Own Town (Finniss Point), South Australia — heart disease
- **Buried:** Strathalbyn Cemetery, South Australia

## Marriage (1): Richard Paynter (1838–1869)

- **Marriage date/location:** Solemnized by John Kither (Officiating Minister) at Chain of Ponds Parsonage. Witnessed by her father Francis Telfer and Henry Whiting of Chain of Ponds. Jean was several months pregnant at the time.
- **Richard Paynter:** Son of Richard Paynter (from Calstock, Cornwall, died Jan 1856 aged 39 after "protracted affliction")
- **Richard's occupation:** Initially a shepherd at Koppio (working for Jean's uncle James Telfer), later a school teacher at Saint Kitts (between Kapunda and Truro) — change due to poor health
- **Richard died:** 7 February 1869, St. Kitts Creek, of pleurisy, aged 30. Newspaper: "Mr Paynter, the Schoolmaster at St. Kitts Creek, died somewhat suddenly on Sunday last, by which a widow and five children have been left unprovided for."

### Children of Richard Paynter and Jean Telfer

#### 1. THOMAS PAYNTER
- **Born:** 22 December 1859, Ward Farm, near Kersbrook
- **Married:** Elizabeth Liebich, 1 December 1881, at Tarcowie
- **Occupation:** Leased/worked farmland at Arden Vale (near Quorn, SA). Later worked properties around Peterborough.
- **Accident:** Slipped under a train, had a leg amputated in 1946
- **Died:** Shortly after amputation in 1946, aged 86. Buried Peterborough Cemetery.
- **Children (9):** Richard, Lilian, Gustav, Ethel, Dinah, Agnes, Rose, Thomas, Helena

##### 1a. Richard William John Paynter
- Born 27 Apr 1882, Mannanarie. Bought own farm at Arden Vale at age 18. Married Lucy Arabella Hill. Died 23 Jul 1960.

##### 1b. Lilian Ellen Jane Paynter
- Born 1885, Arden Vale. Worked on stations. Married (1) Henry Alcock (railway worker, Quorn), (2) Herbert Mayer (station hand), (3) Alfred Hatchard (Iron Knob). Died 1 Mar 1954, Iron Knob.

##### 1c. Gustav Francis George Paynter
- Born 1888. Married (1) Sarah Jane Barbour, (2) Lily Olive Rowe. Worked for railways. Died 1 Jul 1946, aged 58.

##### 1d. Ethel Emily Elizabeth Paynter
- Born 1891, Arden Vale. Married (1) Frank Smith (railway worker — d. 1932), (2) David George Flavel (railway ganger). Died 19 May 1932, Peterborough.

##### 1e. Dinah Alice Mary Paynter
- Born 27 Sep 1894, Arden Vale. Married William Mundy (railway employee). Died 27 May 1963.

##### 1f. Agnes Letitia May Rose Paynter
- Born 1896, Arden Vale. Married George Hucks (railway worker). Died 28 May 1952, buried Loxton.

##### 1g. Rose Isabel Margaret Paynter
- Born 8 Aug 1900, Quorn nursing home. Married John Hunter Rankin (of Koolunga, son of Scottish migrants Angus and Jane Rankin) in 1918. Died 8 Jul 1988, Port Augusta.

##### 1h. Thomas Frederick Edward Paynter
- Born 31 Dec 1903, Arden Vale. Married Florence Catherine Donovan. Died 16 Sep 1940, aged 36.

##### 1i. Helena Florence Daisy Paynter
- Born 19 Aug 1906, Arden Vale. Married Harry Richmond Hill (northern station hand). Lived in Terowie, later Gawler.

#### 2. MARY JANE PAYNTER
- **Born:** 30 June 1861, Koppio (near Port Lincoln)
- **Married:** John Watson, 1 March 1882. Ceremony by Rev. H. Chapman (first Wesleyan Minister of Hawker), witnessed by Mrs Anne Mapleton and John Telfer (Mary's uncle).
- **John Watson:** Grandfather Charles Watson was a convict on "Asia II" (1827, Tasmania). John was a "lime burner" of Arkaba.
- **Lived:** Willow Plains (share-farmed land owned by John Telfer). Moved to Olinda, Victoria in 1910.
- **John died:** 10 September 1929
- **Mary Jane died:** 14 July 1945, Preston, Victoria, aged 84. Buried Fawkner Cemetery.
- **Children (10):** Joseph, Florence Beatrice, Lancelot Hobart, John Francis Percival, Blanche Olive May, Cecil Charles, Clifford, Vera Merle, Royal Ernest, Arthur

#### 3. FRANCIS TELFER PAYNTER
- **Born:** 27 October 1862, Koppio

#### 4. ELIZABETH PAYNTER
- **Born:** 31 December 1864, Chain of Ponds area

#### 5. DINAH FLAVEL PAYNTER
- **Born:** July 1869 (five months after Richard's death)

## Marriage (2): Frederick Parker

- **Marriage date/location:** Christmas Day, 25 December 1871, at Kapunda
- **Frederick Parker:** Son of George Parker. Occupation: itinerant farm labourer / bullock driver
- **Lived:** Hawker, Oraparinna area (far north SA), later Finniss Point
- **Frederick died:** 12 August 1928, Berrima Hospital, NSW. Buried Bowral Cemetery, NSW. In later years he lived with his daughter Margaret and son-in-law Edward Liebich at Wildes Meadow, NSW.
- **At Frederick's death, only 3 of his children survived him:** Margaret, Frederick (known as George), and Joanna

### Children of Frederick Parker and Jean Telfer

#### 1. MARGARET ELIZA PARKER
- **Born:** 26 July 1872, Finniss Point
- **Married:** Edward Liebich (26yo farmer of Arden Vale, son of Gustav Liebich), 22 February 1893, at Wesleyan Parsonage, Quorn
- **Lived:** Moved to Handen, NSW (c.1911), then Robertson and Moss Vale districts
- **Died:** 27 March 1938, Moss Vale. Buried Moss Vale Cemetery.
- **Children (8):** Jean, Alice Mary, Martha Elizabeth, Emily Margaret, Edward Harold, Frederick Walter, Ruth Temperance, Ella

#### 2. FREDERICK GEORGE PARKER (known as George)
- **Born:** 5 April 1874, Oraparinna (father was bullock driver)
- **Occupation:** Living at Wantiool at time of death
- **Never married**
- **Died:** 16 December 1946, Junee Hospital, NSW. Buried Church of England Cemetery, Junee, NSW.

#### 3. ANNIE PARKER
- **Born:** 18 November 1875, Oraparinna
- **Died:** 6 November 1895, Adelaide

#### 4. MARTHA PARKER
- **Born:** January 1878 (estimated from school records — no birth certificate found)
- **School:** Queens Own Town School, attended 1886–1892

#### 5. JOANNA WITTITA CORDLEY PARKER
- **Born:** 6 February 1880, Arkaba
- **Still living** at father's death in 1928

|#### 6. ETHEL MAY PARKER
- **Born:** 4 June 1881, Hawker
- **School:** Until 1895

## Family Stories

### Left a Widow at 29

When Jean's first husband Richard Paynter died of pleurisy in February 1869 at just 30, he left her with five children and no provision. The local paper put it bluntly — "a widow and five children have been left unprovided for." Jean was pregnant with her fifth child Dinah Flavel Paynter, born five months after Richard died. A schoolteacher who'd been in poor health for some time, Richard's passing left the family scrambling.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.76-79)*

### A Christmas Day Wedding

On Christmas Day 1871, Jean — now going by Jane — married Frederick Parker at Kapunda. Frederick was a bullock driver and itinerant farm labourer, and the marriage took Jean and her children from the relative comfort of Finniss Point to the far north of South Australia around Hawker and Oraparinna. Life in the north was hard and isolated.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.77-79)*

### The Roof-Top Refuge

Jean's eldest son Thomas Paynter built a stone house with a thatched roof at Arden Vale near Quorn. When he and his wife Elizabeth had to walk five miles into town for supplies, they'd put the children on the roof of the house — safe from the dingoes and wild dogs that roamed the area. Years later, Thomas lost a leg slipping under a train and died shortly after at 86. The ruins of that stone house still stand among the peppertrees planted in those early days.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.79-81)*

### The Convict Who Built Lighthouses

Jean's daughter Mary Jane Paynter married John Watson, whose grandfather Charles Watson arrived in Tasmania as a convict on the *Asia II* in 1827. Charles was an engineer assigned to Public Works, became Engineer in Charge of building lighthouses around Tasmania — Bruny Island, Swan Island, Goose Island, and Tow Head — and even built the causeway at Bridgewater. He got an unconditional pardon in 1834 after serving just 7 of his 14-year sentence. John himself ran away to sea at 12, served on whaling ships, and was a "lime burner" of Arkaba when he married Mary Jane.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.78-84)*

### End of the Line at Finniss

Jean died of heart disease in 1892 at Queens Own Town (Finniss Point), aged just 51, and was buried at Strathalbyn Cemetery. Her husband Frederick outlived her by 36 years, spending his final days living with his daughter Margaret and son-in-law at Wildes Meadow, New South Wales. He was buried at Bowral in 1928.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.78-84)*|

Born ~1770 at Sorbietrees, Roxburghshire, Scotland. Daughter of James Telfer and Margaret Armstrong of Sorbietrees. Died 9 February 1842 at Newcastleton aged 72. Name appears on the family headstone in Castleton Cemetery. Never married.

## Family Stories

### The Sister on the Stone

Jenet Telfer was born around 1770 at Sorbietrees, Roxburghshire, the daughter of James Telfer and Margaret Armstrong. She never married and lived out her life in the Scottish Borders. She died on 9 February 1842 at Newcastleton at age 72.

Her name sits on the family headstone in Castleton Cemetery, carved alongside her parents and siblings — one of the quiet threads in the Telfer story whose life was lived, marked, and remembered in stone.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.17-19)*

## Family Stories

John Charles Dillon married Elizabeth Beattie Telfer on 18th December 1856. The wedding took place in the home of Elizabeth's uncle, Francis Telfer, at "Macoota" — Section 6146, Chain of Ponds in the Hundred of Para Wirra. John's occupation was listed as "Stock-keeper" and his residence as "Wall — Hundred of Murray". The witnesses were Elizabeth's brothers James and Robert Telfer, and the officiating minister was William Vercoe.

John was the son of John Boswell Dillon, who was a descendant of Viscount Dillon of Ireland. Early in their married life, John and Elizabeth had a property on the Yorke Peninsula, later moved to Tea Tree Gully, and eventually settled at Millbrook.

John was also a trustee of the Church of Christ at Chain of Ponds (the Kersbrook area), listed alongside Francis Telfer on the 1862 land transfer deed from Thomas Scott.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp. 29, 214)*

*Note: Much of the narrative about John and Elizabeth's life together is told through Elizabeth's story.*

# John Smith (~1827–1895)

**Role:** Husband of Esther Jane Telfer — patriarch of the Smith line
**Born:** ~1827 — Copenhagen, Denmark
**Died:** ~1895

John Smith was born in Copenhagen, Denmark, the son of a Scottish Sea Captain and his Danish wife. He married Esther Jane Telfer on 16 November 1863 at the Wesleyan Parsonage in Kapunda, South Australia.

John and Esther had six children: Jane Sophie, Margaret Dougal, Esther Telfer, John James, Francis Telfer, and Elizabeth Anne.

**Source:** *From the Borders to the Bush* — Chapter on Esther Jane Telfer

## Family Stories

John Smith was born in Copenhagen, Denmark around 1830. His father John was a Scottish sea captain and his mother was Danish. After his father's death, John and his mother stayed on in Denmark for some years before moving to Scotland, and eventually they emigrated to South Australia and took up farming in the Barossa Valley.

On 16th November 1863, John married Esther Jane Telfer at the Wesleyan Parsonage in Kapunda. Charles and Elizabeth Farrow (Esther's sister) were witnesses. John was 34 at the time and Esther was 30. They had six children: Jane Sophie, Margaret Dougal (born at Burra), Esther Telfer Smith, John James (born at Tungkillo), Francis Telfer Smith (born at Mount Gambier), and Elizabeth Anne.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, p.35)*

title: John Telfer — Family & Biography

body_markdown:
# John Telfer (1805–1839)

**Role:** Brother of Francis Telfer (1809–1895), stayed in Scotland

John Telfer was born ~1805 at Blackburnfoot, Newcastleton, Roxburghshire, Scotland. He was the sixth child of James Telfer (1761–1845), a hand loom weaver, and Elizabeth "Betty" Hutton (1774–1853).

He died in 1839, aged approximately 34. He did NOT emigrate to Australia. While his brothers Francis and James emigrated to South Australia, John remained in Scotland for his entire life.

He is one of the "Other Children" on the family tree, distinguished from his cousin John in the South Australian branch.

## Family Stories

### The Son on the Headstone

John Telfer was born around 1805 at Blackburnfoot, the little weaving settlement at the northern edge of Newcastleton. He was the sixth child of James Telfer and Betty Hutton, growing up in a cottage where hand looms clacked and the family cow grazed on the hills above town.

Unlike his brothers Francis and James, who would cross the ocean to South Australia, John stayed. He lived and died within sight of where he was born. He died unmarried on 3 March 1839, at age 33, still at Blackburnfoot.

His name was carved on the family headstone in Castleton Cemetery:

> "Also John Telfer their son who died at Blackburnfoot on 3rd March, 1839, aged 33 years."

The headstone also suggests something else. Blackburnfoot — the place where John lived and died — was still there in 1839. But by the time James Telfer died in 1845, the family had moved. Blackburnfoot was demolished when the railway came through in the early 1840s.

So John was the last of the Telfers to die at Blackburnfoot. His siblings scattered — some to Australia, some to other parts of Scotland — but John stayed until the very end. The railway tracks run over his old home now.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.17-20; Castleton Cemetery headstone)*

**Source:** *From the Borders to the Bush* — pages 17–20

# John Telfer (1840–1913)

**Role:** Third son of [[James Telfer (1796–1863)]] to emigrate — founder of the Tantanoola Telfer line
**Born:** 1840 — Peel, Roxburghshire, Scotland
**Died:** 5 January 1913 — Tantanoola, South Australia
**Spouse:** Martha Allen (1842–1876) (m. 1865), Martha Clara Henstridge (1856–1921) (m. 1876)
**Father:** [[James Telfer (1796–1863)]]
**Mother:** Elizabeth Beattie (1802–1891)

## Family

| Relation | Name |
|----------|------|
| **Spouse (1)** | Martha Allen (1842–1876) |
| **Spouse (2)** | Martha Clara Henstridge (1856–1921) |
| **Father** | [[James Telfer (1796–1863)]] |
| **Mother** | Elizabeth Beattie |
| **Brother** | [[James Telfer (1829–1914)]] |
| **Sister** | [[Elizabeth Beattie Telfer (1832–1896)]] — m. Dillon |
| **Brother** | [[Robert Telfer (1835–1907)]] |
| **Brother** | [[Adam Francis Telfer (1842–1925)]] |

## Life Summary

John Telfer was the third son of James and Elizabeth to emigrate to South Australia. He was born at Peel, Roxburghshire in 1840 and followed his siblings in 1859 at age 19. He settled at Tantanoola in the South East, became the first Postmaster, and was a prominent figure in the community. John and his second wife Martha Henstridge built the family that would carry the Telfer name through the next generations.

## Family Stories

John Telfer was born at Peel, Roxburghshire, Scotland in 1840, the third son of James and Elizabeth Telfer. In 1859, five years after his brothers James and Robert had left, and at the age of 19, John followed them to South Australia. He left home with a reference from the Rev. John Fergusson of the Parish of Edgerston, dated 15th June, 1859 — one of the last documents he obtained before sailing. Three days later, on 18th June, 1859, he sailed on the "Morning Star" for a journey of 140 days to Melbourne. The ship carried 111 adults and 13 children. John was listed as a Shepherd, aged 19, from Scotland.

He landed in Melbourne and made his way to South Australia, where he found his Uncle Francis Telfer at "Macoota", Kersbrook. It must have been a happy reunion with his brothers and sister — he hadn't seen them in five years.

John came to South Australia under contract to Mr. Alexander Borthwick Murray. For seven years he worked as a shepherd for Mr. Murray at Tungkillo in the Adelaide Hills. On 19th January, 1865, he married Martha Allen at the private residence of Mr. Robert Boyd in Synagogue Place, Adelaide. The marriage certificate described John as a Shepherd of "full age" and Martha as a spinster, also of "full age". Martha was the daughter of William Allen, born in 1842, and her family are believed to have come from Glenmaquin, County Donegal, Ireland.

John and Martha had four children — James, Elizabeth, Susan and Martha.

The family moved to the South East of the State in 1874 and settled at Tantanoola, then known as Lucieton. But tragedy struck. Martha died on 9th March, 1876 from cancer, leaving John with four children aged 10, 8, 5 and 3. The "Border Watch" recorded her death bluntly: "Death in Hospital: On Thursday morning, Martha Telfer, wife of Mr. John Telfer, of German Flat, died in Hospital in Mount Gambier from cancer. She had not been there long. She was 34 years of age."

John married for the second time on 28th December, 1876 — just nine months after Martha's death, and with four young children to care for. His second wife was Martha Clara Henstridge, daughter of Frederick Henstridge. The marriage took place at John's private residence at Tantanoola Creek, officiated by Rev. Charles Tresize. John was described as a "Stockholder", aged 34, and Martha as a Spinster, aged 23.

Martha Henstridge came from a family with a remarkable heritage. An old letter in the family notes that "we are descended from the Viking Hengest who came to England as a mercenary to assist King Vertigen of Kent. He overthrew Vertigen and ruled Kent for a number of years. His descendants fought the Normans in Sherwood Forest with Robin Hood. The heir to Hengest-Ridge Castle was given a baroncy by King John." The family held the manuscripts to Magna Carta secretly in Hengestridge Castle until King John was forced to sign them. The town of Henstridge is still there, part of the estate held by the Duke of Bedford.

John quickly established himself in Tantanoola. The first town blocks were auctioned in 1879 — John purchased Lot 106 for £2.15.0. In 1888 he bought more lots, and in partnership with his brother Adam and Heinrich Kornor, he purchased several other allotments in 1889. The three were listed as Directors of the Tantanoola Cheese and Butter Venture.

He opened a butcher shop in 1880 but closed it seven years later. He was appointed as the first Postmaster at Tantanoola in 1881, a position he held until 1888. The Post Office operated a daily service to Adelaide, and in 1890 a telegraph service commenced, followed by a money order service in 1891, and a Savings Bank Agency in 1893.

In 1894, when the Tantanoola Cheese and Butter Venture failed, John purchased the factory, the land and the plant for £170 — it had originally cost £1,000. The price of milk at that time was 2½d per gallon, but a neighbouring factory paid 3d, so farmers carted their milk by horse and dray an extra five miles for the extra halfpenny.

John was Chairman of the Tantanoola Drainage Board, a member of the Tantanoola District Council, and on the committee that formed the Presbyterian Church in Tantanoola — the church was built on land that John gave. He purchased grazing land near Tantanoola, named his property "Brackenridge", and farmed there until his son Mark took over. John retired to a house in the township where he lived until his death.

His obituary in the South Eastern Times on 10th January, 1913 noted: "For several years he was in the employ of Mr. A.B. Murray at Tungkillo. He came to Tantanoola in 1874 and for many years carried on a butchery and storekeeping business very successfully, but of late years he had been in poor health. He was a member of the first district council of Tantanoola. Deceased leaves a widow and large family of sons and daughters."

John Telfer died on Sunday, 5th January, 1913, aged 72. He is buried at Tantanoola Cemetery alongside his second wife Martha Clara, who died in 1921. Her memorial card read: "The Lord giveth and the Lord taketh away; blessed be the name of the Lord."

Some of John's descendants still live and farm in the Tantanoola district to this day.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp. 233–240)*

## Sources

- **Source:** Donald Telfer, *From the Borders to the Bush* (ISBN 0 7316 6387 X), pp. 36–37
- South Eastern Times, 10 January 1913 — obituary
- Border Watch, 11 March 1876 — death of Martha Allen Telfer

body_markdown:
# John Telfer (1847–1929)

**Role:** Mark's great-great-grandfather — son of the Scottish immigrant
**Born:** 28 May 1847 — Adelaide, South Australia
**Died:** 23 August 1929 (aged 82) — Clare, South Australia
**Buried:** Clare Cemetery, Clare, South Australia
**Occupation:** Farmer — 47 years at Willow Plains
**Residence:** Willow Plains (near Clare), South Australia
**Grandson:** [[Murray John Telfer (1924–2009)]]
**Great-grandson:** [[Timothy Neil Telfer (1959–?)]]
**Great-great-grandson:** [[Mark Telfer (1877–1946)]]

---

## Family Stories

### The Horse-Drawn Van and the School Mistress

John Telfer was born in Adelaide on 28 May 1847, the eldest surviving son of Scottish immigrant Francis Telfer and his third wife Margaret Wright. He grew up at Chain of Ponds and Kersbrook in the Adelaide Hills, learning to farm from his father.

As a young man, John didn't just sell fruit and veg locally — he loaded his horse-drawn van and made regular runs to Kadina and beyond, peddling produce to the miners and settlers up north. It was on one of these trips that his uncle decided John needed a wife. The uncle told him to call at Tarlee school next time he was passing and make the acquaintance of the school mistress, Miss Caroline Amelia Masters. John took the advice — and kept going back.

Caroline wasn't just any school marm. She'd started a school at Gilberton, then when the railway bypassed the hotel by two miles, Tarlee sprang up at the rail head and she moved there. By 1870 she was teaching 41 pupils in the Baptist Church. She resigned on 17 August 1874 to marry John.

On the marriage certificate she signed as C.A. Masters — she later dropped the "A" because she didn't want her initials to be C.A.T. Telfer.

### Willow Plains and the One-Room Hut

When the government cancelled grazing leases in the north and cut the land into small farming blocks, Caroline urged John to apply. He was allotted two sections in the Hundred of Arkaba. In March 1878 he set out by wagon with a camp oven, billy can, water bags, blankets, horse feed, seed wheat and farm tools. He built a one-roomed wood and iron hut with a stone chimney, then went back for his family.

Caroline and the three children travelled later by spring dray — a three-month-pregnant mother on a long, jolting journey. The hut had a hessian partition dividing bedroom from living quarters. Minimum furniture. This was home.

Their son Ernest John was born in that hut on 2 September 1878 — the first white baby born at Willow Plains. The midwife scolded Caroline for opening a window for air: "You wicked woman! Are you trying to kill that poor little baby by giving it a chill?"

### Water and the Angle Farm

John's first problem was water — the nearest well was five miles away. He dug a first well — a failure. The second struck good supply at about 50 feet, and from that moment the farm began to establish itself. A permanent stone house was begun and practically completed by 1893 — still in use today.

The property was called Angle Farm because the boundaries formed all sorts of odd shapes — a triangle with a square attached.

### The Double Bereavement

John and Caroline farmed at Willow Plains for 47 years. They raised six sons and adopted two children whose mother had died. In a remarkable turn, John died on 23 August 1929 at age 82, and Caroline followed him the next day. The Register News-Pictorial ran a photo: "THE LATE MRS. JOHN TELFER, of Clare, who died within a few hours of her husband. Both were prominent Clare residents."

They were buried together at Clare Cemetery.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.109-118; Trove newspaper archives)*

---

## Family

| Relation | Name |
|----------|------|
| **Mother** | [[Margaret Wright Telfer (?–1892)]] |
| **Father** | [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]] |
| **Spouse** | [[Caroline Amelia Telfer (1842–1929)]] (née Masters, m. 22 Sep 1874) |
| **Children** | [[Francis Charles Telfer (1875–1954)]], Ernest John Telfer, William James Telfer, Albert George Telfer, Walter William Telfer, Edwin Gilbert Telfer |
| **Siblings** | George Wright Telfer, Margaret Dougal Telfer |
| **Half-siblings** | James Telfer, Esther Smith, Elizabeth Farrow, Jane Telfer |

---

## Life Story

John Telfer was born in **Adelaide, South Australia** on **28 May 1847** — the eldest surviving son of Scottish immigrant [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)|Francis Telfer]] and his third wife Margaret Wright. He grew up on the family farm at Chain of Ponds and Kersbrook in the Adelaide Hills.

On **22 September 1874**, he married **Caroline Amelia Masters** at the Baptist Chapel, Tarlee. The marriage was announced in the South Australian Register. Caroline had immigrated from England as a young child with her family aboard the *Templar* in 1845.

John and Caroline settled at **Willow Plains, near Clare**, where they farmed for **47 years**. They raised six sons:

1. [[Francis Charles Telfer (1875–1954)]] (1875–1954) — Mark's great-grandfather
2. Ernest John Telfer (1878–1953)
3. William James Telfer (1880–?)
4. Albert George Telfer (1881–?)
5. Walter William Telfer (1884–1966)
6. Edwin Gilbert Telfer (1887–?)

John was described as a **prominent Clare resident** and was actively associated with every community move in the Willow Plains district. He was a **prominent member of the Methodist Church**, serving as **superintendent of the Sunday-school for about 30 years** (per both Advertiser and Chronicle obituaries).

### The Double Bereavement — 1929

In a remarkable and tragic turn, **John and Caroline died within hours of each other** in August 1929. John passed away on **23 August 1929** at age 82, and Caroline followed him **the next day**, 24 August 1929. The *Register News-Pictorial* ran a photo with the headline:

> "THE LATE MRS. JOHN TELFER, of Clare, who died within a few hours of her husband. Both were prominent Clare residents."

They were buried together at **Clare Cemetery**.

As the Advertiser obituary noted:
> "He was a resident of Willow Plains for 47 years. He was actively associated with every movement inaugurated for the wellbeing of the district, and was a prominent member of the Methodist Church and Sunday-school. Mr. Telfer held the position of superintendent of the Sunday-school for about 30 years."

---

| ~1882–1929 | Farmed at Willow Plains, Clare (47 years) |

| 25 Aug 1929 | Buried at Clare Cemetery |

---

## Photos

![Telfer family reunion, circa 1920](../_assets/Telfer family reunion c1920.jpg)

*Telfer family reunion, circa 1920. Large multi-generational group portrait of ~25 individuals. John Telfer (1847–1929, aged ~73) seated center-left with full white beard, dark suit, and watch chain visible on vest. Caroline Amelia Telfer (1842–1929, aged ~78) seated center-right in dark dress with white lace collar, white hair pulled back. Their son Francis Charles 'Charlie' Telfer (1875–1954, aged ~45) and wife Amy Ellen Telfer (1884–1951, aged ~36) among the standing adults with their children and grandchildren. Studio setting with textured wallpaper backdrop on left, dark curtain on right.*

Find a Grave memorial: [John Telfer (1847–1929)](https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/200328650/john-telfer) — Clare Cemetery. Headstone photo not yet obtained.

---

## Sources

### The Horse-Drawn Van to Kadina

Born 24th May 1847, John spent his early years helping his father Francis grow and sell fruit and vegetables. They didn't just depend on the local market — John, in his horse-drawn van, made regular trips to Kadina and beyond to peddle their home-grown produce to the miners and settlers up north.

### The Uncle's Matchmaking

In the early 1870s, one of John's uncles decided it was time the young man settled down. He suggested John should call at Tarlee school next time he was travelling through, and make the acquaintance of the school mistress, Miss Caroline Amelia Masters. Being a dutiful nephew, John took the advice — and seemed to like what he saw, because he kept going back.

### Caroline the Teacher

Caroline Masters was no ordinary school marm. She first tried opening a school at Gilberton with her sister, near the Forrester's Arms Hotel — a staging camp for bullockies hauling goods to and from Adelaide. When the railway bypassed the hotel by two miles and the town of Tarlee sprang up at the rail head, the school failed.

In 1870 she tried again, this time granted a licence by the Tarlee District Council. She started teaching in the original section of the Baptist Church with 41 pupils — 18 boys and 23 girls. The Tarlee school history says she showed "dedication and persistence that would do a present day teacher proud." She taught there until 17th August 1874, when she resigned to marry John.

### The C.A.T. Problem

On the marriage certificate Caroline signed as C.A. Masters. In later years she removed the A from Amelia because she was not keen on her initials being C.A.T. Telfer. From then on she was simply C.M. Telfer.

### On the Death of Little John Ernest

John and Caroline's second son, John Ernest, was born 1st March 1877 and lived only six months, dying of pneumonia on 20th September. Caroline wrote a heart-wrenching poem that included these lines:

> "Safe in the arms of Jesus,
> Safe on His gentle breast —
> But my arms are empty, my heart is sad,
> And my spirit cannot rest."

> "Not much to lose a baby,
> The unknowing world may say;
> May they never know what my heart has known,
> Nor feel what I feel today."

### The Adopted Children

Before leaving Kersbrook, John and Caroline offered to care for two children — a girl about three and her brother, several years older. Their mother had died and their father, a Swiss immigrant, didn't know how to care for four children. Legal adoption wasn't available in South Australia at that time, but John and Caroline assumed full responsibility. The little girl was Bertha, henceforth always known as Bertha Telfer. She became a beloved sister to the boys.

### The Move to Willow Plains

When the SA Government decided to cancel grazing leases in the Northern Districts and cut the land into small farming blocks, Caroline urged John to apply. After interviews he was allotted two sections in the Hundred of Arkaba. He travelled north, built a small one-roomed wood and iron hut with a stone chimney, then returned to Kersbrook.

In March 1878 he set out again by wagon with all the conveniences of the day: camp oven, billy can, water bags, blankets, horse feed, seed wheat and farm tools. He spent the night at Palmers Creek, about 15 miles from his new home, where a Mr Will Sweet and his brother Arthur were camped with their bullock teams. Next morning Sweet recalled being woken by the sound of a shovel — John was digging two trenches through deep sand for his wagon wheels. Sweet told him not to bother — they pulled him across with the bullocks.

Caroline and the three children travelled later by spring dray, likely driven by John's brother George. A three-month-pregnant mother with three children on a long, slow, jolting journey.

They settled into the one-roomed hut with a hessian partition dividing bedroom from living quarters, minimum furniture and equipment — and this became home.

### Ernest John — First White Baby at Willow Plains

On 2nd September 1878, five months after arriving, little Ernest John was born in that hut. A local mid-wife attended. At one stage, while the mid-wife was out of the room, Caroline felt distressed and opened the small window to get fresh air. The mid-wife came storming back: *"You wicked woman! Are you trying to kill that poor little baby by giving it a chill?"* and very decisively shut the window. The child survived and made history as the first white baby born at Willow Plains.

### Digging for Water

With no permanent springs, John's first problem was water. The nearest well was five miles away. He dug a first well under the fence between his and George's blocks — a failure. The second, near the centre of Section 72E, struck a good supply at about 50 feet. From that moment the farm began to establish itself around the water supply. A permanent stone house was begun, added to as finances allowed, and virtually completed in its basic form by 1893. The house is still in use today.

### Angle Farm

When asked why John and Caroline called their property Angle Farm, a glance at the land boundaries explains it — John owned a sort of triangle with a square attached, and even including George's blocks, the boundary contained all sorts of angles.

### Caroline's Brick Oven

Caroline was not keen on iron stoves for baking. She had a brick oven built onto her kitchen — the oven itself outside, but the door opening into the kitchen. About five feet square, half-filled with dirt and stones, then a layer of bricks leaving a two-foot-high oven. She'd build a hot fire while the bread was rising, scrape out the coals and ashes, place in the bread, and wait. It baked beautifully. Cakes, biscuits, pies and tarts the same way.

### Cocky the Wonder Bird

The family had a pet cockatoo who was famously talkative — so important a member of the household that Caroline wrote a poem about him:

> Our Cocky is a wonderous bird,
> Well worthy of a ditty;
> And were his name unknown to fame,
> 'Twere certainly a pity.

When the boys overslept, Cocky called them by name — "Albert! Ernest! Charley!" When horses came home from work he called "Whoa!" When strangers called he'd ask *"You're going to the Band of Hope?"* And when the children came home from school he'd rattle off "Walter! Eddie! Eddie! Walter!" until they came rushing in.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.109-118)*

## Life Summary

Julia Matilda Seebohm was born on 18 October 1876 at Tantanoola, South Australia, the tenth of eleven children of German immigrant Wilhelm Seebohm and Scottish-born Mary Anne McIntyre. Her father Wilhelm emigrated from Altona, near Hamburg, Germany; her mother Mary was from Glasgow, Scotland.

On 9 July 1902, Julia married [[Mark Telfer (1877–1946)]] at the Public Hall, Tantanoola. The marriage was recorded in the local newspaper as uniting "Mr. Mark Telfer, son of Mr. John Telfer, to Miss Matilda Seebohm, daughter of Mr. W. Seebohm." Julia was known in the family as Matilda or Tilly.

She and Mark raised four children at Tantanoola and North Millicent: Floris, Kenneth, Melvin, and adopted son Murray. The family lived in the Tantanoola area, a small farming community in the Wattle Range Council region of South Australia's South East.

Julia died on 26 April 1939 and was buried at Tantanoola Cemetery. She predeceased her husband Mark, who died in 1946; his death notice in The Advertiser referred to him as "beloved husband of the late Julia Matilda Telfer."

Kenneth William John Telfer (the book records his middle names as William John, not Alexander) was born in 1904, the second child and eldest son of Mark Telfer (1877–1946) and Julia Matilda Seebohm (1876–1939) of Tantanoola, South Australia.

He married Jessie Sargent. Their son, Murray, married Susanne Maloney and had five children — Joanne, Mark (who married Maryann Harrap), John, Richard and Neville.

Ken played football for Tantanoola for many years. He was Captain of the team and played at centre. He also played in the Tantanoola cricket team, being a useful bat and a slow bowler. In later years he played bowls, both indoor and outdoor. He held the position of President of the Tantanoola Pastoral, Agricultural and Horticultural Society from 1953–55.

## Family Stories

Ken was the second child and eldest son of Mark and Tillie Telfer. The family history records that he played football for Tantanoola for many years, serving as Captain and playing at centre. He also played cricket for Tantanoola, a useful bat and a slow bowler. In later years he took up bowls, both indoor and outdoor. He served as President of the Tantanoola Pastoral, Agricultural and Horticultural Society from 1953 to 1955. He married Jessie Sargent and they had a son, Murray, who married Susanne Maloney. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.243)*

body_markdown:
# Margaret Dougal Telfer (1849–1936)

**Role:** Daughter of Francis and Margaret — the one who married her cousin and raised a dozen kids in the South East

**Born:** 1849 — Kersbrook, South Australia
**Died:** 7 November 1936 — Knightsbridge, South Australia
**Spouse:** Adam Francis Telfer (m. 25 March 1868)
**Children:** 12

---

## Family

| Relation | Name |
|----------|------|
| **Mother** | [[Margaret Wright Telfer (?–1892)]] |
| **Father** | [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]] |
| **Spouse** | [[Adam Francis Telfer (1842–1925)]] |
| **Siblings** | [[John Telfer (1847–1929)]], [[George Wright Telfer (1850–1913)]] |

---

## Family Stories

### Married at Eighteen

Margaret was just 18 when she married her cousin Adam Francis Telfer on 25th March 1868. The wedding was at her father's home, "Macoota", Kersbrook. Her cousins George and Mary Robertson witnessed, along with Adam's brother John. Adam was described as a "Stockholder" from Koppio, Port Lincoln. The Rev. John Kither performed the ceremony. Margaret was the youngest of the children still at home — the year before, her brother John had married Caroline Masters in the same house. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.268)*

### Twelve Children

Margaret didn't have an easy life. She had twelve children over twenty-two years, the first born at Koppio in 1869 and the last at Tantanoola in 1891. The first, Margaret Wright Telfer, died of pneumonia just before her twenty-first birthday — she was supposed to get a piano as a present but never lived to see it. That's the kind of loss that never leaves a mother. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.268)*

### Edgerston at Tantanoola

After years at Koppio, Adam and Margaret moved the family to the South East in the early 1870s. They settled at Tantanoola (then called Lucieton), where Adam opened a store in 1880. They built a home they called "Edgerston," and there Margaret raised the bulk of her enormous family. The town was growing fast — Millicent and Mount Muirhead were described in glowing terms as a "great plain... dotted with substantial homesteads." The Telfers were right in the middle of it all. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.269-272)*

### The Farewell That Broke Them

In 1908, after nearly thirty years in Tantanoola, Adam and Margaret decided to move to Adelaide. The people of the district presented them with a silver tea service — it's still in the possession of their great-grandson, Bruce Watson of Millicent, as of 1986. When the train pulled into the station to take them away, a crowd gathered on the platform and sang "God be with you till we meet again." It was too much for their daughter Eva, who gathered her son Rex in her arms and boarded the train without looking back. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.272-275)*

### The Quiet Years at Knightsbridge

They settled in at "Waverley Park," Lower Mitcham, then moved to "Edgerston House" on Rochester Street, Knightsbridge in 1916. The nine-roomed house sat in large grounds with a creek running through the garden and a wooden bridge covered in wisteria. They had an extensive orchard and kept fowls and ducks. Margaret and the girls got involved with the Knightsbridge Baptist Church — the girls taught Sunday School and Hazel sang in the choir. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.275)*

### Nursing Adam

After Adam's stroke in 1919, Margaret nursed him for years. His left arm and hand were useless, his eyesight was failing. He'd dictate letters and she'd finish them for him — "Father has left this so I will close it for him. Best love from us all. M.D.T." She was his hands and his eyes through those long years. He died in 1925. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.275-276)*

### The Matriarch in Black

In her later years Margaret developed cataracts and went blind. Her daughter Violet cared for her, guiding her to her special chair by the dining room window. She always wore a long black dress, and that's how her many grandchildren remember her. On fine days she'd sit on the verandah, the matriarch of the Telfer clan, holding court. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.277)*

### The Telfer Grand Central

The house at Knightsbridge never stopped. Sons, daughters, grandchildren, cousins, friends, neighbours — everyone was welcome. Several grandchildren boarded there while studying at the Adelaide Teachers College. The place was a base for all branches of the Telfer Clan whenever they visited Adelaide. Margaret kept up the traditional Telfer hospitality, and there was always a constant stream of visitors. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.277)*

### Psalm 46

In October 1936, Margaret slipped beside her chair and broke her hip. The last days of her life were filled with pain. Her daughter Violet wrote three heartbreaking letters to sister Effie in Perth describing it all. Margaret died on 7th November 1936, aged 87. She's buried at Mitcham Cemetery alongside Adam, with the words "God is our Refuge and Strength" from her favourite Psalm 46 on the headstone — a fitting tribute to a woman of quiet strength who raised twelve children and outlived her husband by eleven years. *(From the Borders to the Bush, p.277)*

---

## Life Story

Margaret Dougal Telfer was the daughter of Francis Telfer and Margaret Wright, born at Kersbrook in 1849. At 18 she married her cousin Adam Francis Telfer. She raised twelve children across Koppio, Tantanoola, and Knightsbridge, nursing her husband through a long illness after his stroke. She died in 1936 at the age of 87, buried at Mitcham Cemetery.

**Source:** *From the Borders to the Bush* — pages 268-277

# Margaret Telfer (1802–1884)

**Role:** Sister of Francis Telfer (1809–1895), stayed in Scotland

Margaret Telfer was born ~1802 at Blackburnfoot, Newcastleton, Roxburghshire, Scotland. She was the fifth child of James Telfer (1761–1845), a hand loom weaver, and Elizabeth "Betty" Hutton (1774–1853).

She did NOT emigrate to Australia and died in 1884 in Scotland.

The book states: *"We have no further information about four members of this family; namely Isobel, Adam, Margaret and William."* Like her siblings Isobel, Adam, and William, Margaret's fate after the family records is not documented beyond her death.

**Source:** *From the Borders to the Bush* — pages 17–20

---

## Family Stories

### Stayed Behind

Margaret Telfer was born around 1802 at Blackburnfoot, Newcastleton — the fifth child of James Telfer and Elizabeth Hutton. While her brothers Francis and John crossed the ocean to South Australia, Margaret stayed in Scotland. She never emigrated and died there in 1884.

Like her siblings Isobel, Adam, and William, the book has no further record of her life. But her death in Scotland tells its own story — while a new branch of the family took root on the other side of the world, Margaret remained in the valley she was born in, part of the old world that the emigrants left behind.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.17-20)*

## Life Summary

Margaret Wright was the **third wife** of [[Francis Telfer (1809–1895)]]. She married him in South Australia after the deaths of his first wife Jean Murray (d. 1839) and second wife Dinah Flavel.

She was the mother of:
- **[[John Telfer (1847–1929)]]** — Mark's great-great-grandfather
- **George Wright Telfer** — who later farmed at Willaston
- **Margaret Dougal Telfer**

Margaret Wright died on **13 September 1892** at Kersbrook and is buried at Kersbrook Cemetery (General, Section B, Row 1, Plot B13). Her death came about **three years before Francis**, which prompted his eventual move from the farm at Kersbrook to live with his son at Gawler.

---

## About the Three Wives of Francis Telfer

Francis Telfer married three times — an unusual number that sometimes causes confusion in genealogical records:

1. **Jean Murray** — married in Scotland, mother of James (1832), Esther Jane (1834), Elizabeth (1836). Jean died 22 Jan 1839, shortly after arrival in SA.
2. **Dinah Flavel** — second wife in South Australia
3. **Margaret Wright** — third wife and mother of John and the younger children

Some trees simply list "Margaret Telfer" as Francis's wife without specifying which marriage, leading to contradictions between sources.

## Family Stories

### The Stirling Castle Legend

> *According to Donald Telfer's family history (1986), Chapter 2, p. 27:* Family tradition held that Margaret Wright was "born in Stirling Castle." Which room — the main bedchamber, a guest room, or the servants' quarters — was left for speculation. The last reigning monarch to live at Stirling Castle was James VI (1567–1625), so the story may refer to her family's residence within the castle precincts rather than the royal apartments.

- WikiTree: [Francis Telfer (abt.1809–1895)](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Telfer-400) — confirms three wives
- RootsWeb Tarlee Cemetery listing — confirms wives' names
- Geni: [John Telfer (1847–1929)](https://www.geni.com/people/John-Telfer/6000000130189316856) — confirms mother Margaret Telfer

## Life Summary

Maria Clara Telfer was the second child of John Telfer and his second wife Martha Clara Henstridge, born around 1878. She was the elder sister of ten siblings from this marriage and was named with the middle name Clara after her mother. She died young, on 22 December 1903 at Tantanoola, South Australia, at approximately 25 years of age, never having married. She predeceased both her mother (who died in 1921) and father (who died in 1913) by ten and eight years respectively — an unusually early passing that cut short a life that might have continued long enough to see the family's later expansion.

## Family Stories

Maria Clara Telfer was the seventh child of John Telfer and the second child of his marriage to Martha Clara Henstridge. She died young at just 25 years of age, never having married. Her memorial card — printed in black with gold lettering — bore her photograph circled with the poignant words "Though lost to sight, To memory dear." Below the photograph was inscribed: "In Loving Memory of Maria Clara Telfer." Her early passing in December 1903 at Tantanoola was a sadness visited upon the family well before her mother's death in 1921 and her father's in 1913.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.242, 248–249)*

## Life Summary

Mark Telfer was born on 12 April 1877 at Up and Down Rocks, South Australia, the first biological child of John Telfer (1840–1913) and his second wife Martha Clara Henstridge. He was the eldest of eleven children from the second marriage.

He married Julia Matilda Seebohm on 9 July 1902. Together they had seven children: Floris Ethel Victoria (1904–1951), Kenneth William John (1904–?), Gilbert Melville known as Mel (1911–1978), Jean Maryann Martha (1910–1984), Joyce Elizabeth (1912–2012), Maifie Beryl (1913–1948), and Lindsay Roland (1920–1976).

The book *From the Borders to the Bush* confirms all seven, listing them as: Floris, Ken, Mel, Jean, Joyce, Maifie and Lindsay.

Mark died on 23 July 1946 in Adelaide, South Australia, at age 69. His death location (Adelaide, not Tantanoola) suggests he may have moved from the family's Tantanoola home base later in life.

## Family Stories

Mark Telfer was John Telfer's sixth child — the first born to his second wife, Martha Clara Henstridge. He married Julia Matilda Seebohm (known as Tillie) in the Tantanoola Public Hall on 9 July 1902, with the Rev. James Davies officiating. Both Mark and Tillie were active in Sunday School teaching at the Tantanoola Presbyterian Church, and the congregation presented them with a large family Bible on their Silver Wedding anniversary.

Mark took over his father's farm, "Brackenridge", when John retired, growing crops and running sheep and cattle. He lived there until about 1940, then purchased a house in Millicent and retired with two of his daughters, Jean and Maifie. Mark was a fine sportsman — he played football and cricket, served as Timekeeper for the football club when his sons took the field, and was a capable batsman and slow bowler who won a medal for the highest batting average in the Tantanoola Cricket Club. He and Tillie raised seven children: Floris, Ken, Mel, Jean, Joyce, Maifie and Lindsay.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.240–241)*

## Life Summary

Martha Allen married John Telfer on 10 January 1865 at the Residence of Robert Boyd, Adelaide, South Australia. She bore four children between 1866 and 1873 — three daughters and one son — before dying young at German Flat, near Mount Gambier, on 9 May 1876, aged approximately 36.

Her death left John Telfer a widower with four young children (the youngest, Martha, was barely three). John remarried seven months later to Martha Clara Henstridge on 28 December 1876.

**Place of origin, parents, migration, and burial location are all unknown.** She may have arrived in South Australia aboard the *Morning Star* (departed Liverpool 28 November 1862, arrived Port Adelaide 13 February 1863) as an unmarried servant, but this is unconfirmed.

## Family Stories

Martha Allen married John Telfer on 19th January 1865. The ceremony took place at the private residence of Mr Robert Boyd in Synagogue Place, Adelaide. On the marriage certificate John was described as a Shepherd of "full age" and Martha as a spinster, also of "full age". Martha was the daughter of William Allen, born in 1842, and her parents are believed to have come from Glenmaquin, County Donegal, Ireland.

John and Martha had four children — James, Elizabeth, Susan and Martha. The family moved to the South East of the state in 1874 and settled at Tantanoola, then known as Lucieton.

Sadly, Martha died on 9th March 1876 at German Flat, leaving John with four children aged 10, 8, 5 and 3. Her death was recorded in the Border Watch on 11th March 1876 with a brief and blunt notice: "Death in Hospital: On Thursday morning, Martha Telfer, wife of Mr. John Telfer, of German Flat, died in Hospital in Mount Gambier from cancer. She had not been there long. She was 34 years of age."

It's a stark statement, and we can only imagine the pain and suffering Martha endured before her untimely death.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, p.234)*

# Martha Henstridge (~1854–1921)

**Role:** Second wife of John Telfer (1840–1913)

After the death of his first wife Martha Allen (1840–1876), John Telfer (1840–1913) married Martha Clara Henstridge on 28 Dec 1876 at the Residence of J. Telfer, Tantanoola Creek, South Australia.

**Born:** 22 Jan 1854, South Australia
**Died:** 13 Nov 1921, Adelaide, South Australia (aged 67)
**Buried:** Tantanoola Cemetery, Tantanoola SA

Martha was the daughter of Frederick Henstridge Sr. and Maria Smith. She had 10 children with John Telfer: Mark, Maria Clara, Isabella Lucieton, John Roland, Clara Blanche, Robert Freddy, Douglas, Colin Roy, Alan Dale, and Alma Tressy.

**Sources:**
1. **WikiTree:** [Martha Clara Henstridge (Henstridge-4)](https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Henstridge-4) — birth 22 Jan 1854, marriage 28 Dec 1876, death 13 Nov 1921 (GenealogySA records)
2. **FindAGrave:** [Martha Clara Telfer (memorial 186972464)](https://www.findagrave.com/memorial/186972464/martha-clara-telfer) — burial at Tantanoola Cemetery
3. **GenealogySA:** Death record Ade sym H B 450 P 228 — Martha died 13 Nov 1921, aged 68, widow, of Tantanoola
4. **Book:** *From the Borders to the Bush*

## Family Stories

After the death of his first wife, John Telfer married for the second time on 28th December 1876. His second wife was Martha Clara Henstridge, daughter of Frederick Henstridge. The marriage took place at John's private residence at Tantanoola Creek, officiated by the Rev. Charles Tresize. John was described as a "Stockholder", aged 34, and Martha as a Spinster, aged 23.

Martha came from a family with a remarkable history. An old letter preserved in the family tells the story: "When John Telfer took Martha Henstridge to wife, he married into a family with a great historic heritage." The Henstridge family is descended from the Viking Hengest, who came to England as a mercenary to assist King Vertigen of Kent, but overthrew him and ruled Kent for a number of years. His descendants fought the Normans in Sherwood Forest with Robin Hood. The heir to Hengest-Ridge Castle was given a baroncy by King John, and the barons kept the manuscripts to Magna Carta secretly in Hengestridge Castle until the King was forced to sign them.

Martha was very supportive of her husband in all his activities. She was an active member of the Tantanoola Red Cross, and served as Postmistress at Tantanoola from 1919 to 1921 after her daughter Tressic. Martha died in 1921 and is buried alongside John at Tantanoola Cemetery, where her headstone reads: "Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord."

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp. 238–240)*

## Life Summary

Martha Telfer was born on 18 April 1873 at Black Heath (also recorded as Blackheath), Tungkillo, South Australia, the fourth child and third daughter of John Telfer (1840–1913) by his first wife [[Martha Allen (1840–1876)]]. The family lived at Honeysuckle Flat and Black Heath during her early years before moving to the Tantanoola district in the South East.

On 29 March 1899 at Tantanoola, SA, Martha married Malcolm Duncan Cameron (1873–1935), a farmer. They had at least one known child: a son, Malcolm Murray Cameron, born 2 August 1905 at Mount Gambier SA.

Martha died on 4 August 1964 at Mount Gambier, South Australia, aged 91, and was predeceased by her husband by 29 years. Her burial location has not been positively identified — no FindAGrave record has been found, and her 1964 death was too late for Trove newspaper death notices.

## Family Stories

Martha — known as Mattie — was the fourth and youngest child of John Telfer and his first wife Martha Allen, born on 18 April 1873 at Black Heath. She married Malcolm Duncan Cameron on 29 March 1899 at Tantanoola. Malcolm was a man of public affairs: during his time in Parliament he served on the Works Committee, eventually becoming its Chairman, and was a lifelong member of the Liberal Party. He was also an Elder of the Presbyterian Church for thirty years.

Mattie and Malcolm raised five children — Murray, Ivan, Lorna, Mavis and Jack — in the South East district. Malcolm died on 1 March 1935, and Mattie lived on for another twenty-nine years, passing away at Mount Gambier in 1964 at the age of 91.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.238–239)*

body_markdown:
# Richard Paynter (1838–1869)

**Role:** First husband of Jean Telfer
**Born:** ~1838 — Cornwall, England
**Died:** 7 February 1869 (aged 30) — St. Kitts Creek, pleurisy
**Buried:** Kapunda area

Richard Paynter was born in Cornwall, England, the son of Richard Paynter of Calstock. He emigrated to South Australia where he worked as a labourer at Chain of Ponds.

He married Jean Telfer on 12 September 1859 at the Chain of Ponds Parsonage, solemnised by John Kither and witnessed by her father Francis Telfer and Henry Whiting. Jean was several months pregnant at the time.

After their first child Thomas was born, the family moved to Koppio near Port Lincoln where Richard worked as a shepherd for Jean's cousin James Telfer. They later returned to the Chain of Ponds area and then to St. Kitts between Kapunda and Truro, where Richard became the local school teacher — a change brought on by his failing health.

Richard died of pleurisy at the age of 30, leaving a widow and five children unprovided for.

**Source:** *From the Borders to the Bush* — Chapter on Jean/Jane Telfer

## Family Stories

Richard Paynter was born in Calstock, Cornwall, the son of Richard Paynter, who died in January 1856 aged 39 after "a protracted affliction." Richard the younger emigrated to South Australia and worked as a labourer at Chain of Ponds. On 12 September 1859, at just 19 years old, Jean Telfer married 21-year-old Richard Paynter at the Chain of Ponds Parsonage — a different setting from her sisters, who were married in their father Francis's home. Jean was several months pregnant at the time. After their first son Thomas was born, the family moved to Koppio near Port Lincoln, where Richard worked as a shepherd for Jean's cousin James Telfer. They later returned to the Chain of Ponds area and eventually settled at St. Kitts, between Kapunda and Truro. There, as Richard's health began to fail, he made an unusual career change — from shepherd to school teacher. The book records that he died of pleurisy on 7 February 1869 at St. Kitts Creek, aged just 30, leaving his widow and five children unprovided for. An in memoriam notice was placed in a local newspaper. His first child Dinah was born at Finniss Point five months after his death.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, p.16)*

# Robert Telfer (1803–1878)

**Role:** Son of the Scottish patriarch — stayed in Castleton, Roxburghshire his entire life  
**Born:** 25 April 1803 — Castleton, Roxburghshire, Scotland  
**Died:** 1878 (aged 74) — Castleton, Scottish Borders, Scotland  
**Buried:** Likely Old Castleton Cemetery, Newcastleton, Scottish Borders, Scotland  
**Occupation:** Farm servant / agricultural labourer

---

## Family Stories

### The Brother Who Stayed — A Life in Castleton

Of all the children of James Telfer and Betty Hutton, Robert was the one who lived and died within a few miles of where he was born. While his younger brother Francis crossed the world to South Australia, and his older brother James followed years later, Robert stayed put in the Liddesdale valley.

He married Elizabeth "Betty" Oliver around 1828 and they set up house in Castleton. The 1841 census shows them with four young children — Elizabeth, James, Jean, and John — living alongside an older John Telfer (64), Violet Telfer, and William Telfer. Extended family sharing a roof, as folks did in those days.

Robert worked as an agricultural labourer, the kind of life his father had lived as a hand loom weaver — hard work, modest means, family close. By 1851, things had changed. Robert was 46 and living with only two of his children still at home. His wife Betty was gone — whether she'd died or left, the records don't say.

He died in 1878 at age 74, in the same parish where he was born. The statutory death registration records his mother's maiden name as Hutton, confirming his place in the family.

Robert never saw Australia. Never sailed on a ship across the ocean. But his story matters too — the brother who stayed, kept the old name in the old country, and lived the quiet life that his more adventurous siblings left behind.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp.17-20; 1841 and 1851 Scotland Censuses)*

## Life Summary

Robert Telfer was born in 1803 in Castleton, Roxburghshire, the fifth child and third son of James Telfer and Betty Hutton. He was baptised on 25 April 1803 in the Church of Scotland at Castleton parish, the same Liddesdale valley where the Telfer family had lived for generations.

Unlike his younger brother Francis, who emigrated to South Australia in 1838, Robert remained in the Scottish Borders his entire life. He married Elizabeth "Betty" Oliver around 1828. The 1841 census shows the couple living in Castleton with their young family, alongside Robert's older brother John Telfer (64), Violet Telfer (25), and William Telfer (22) — likely extended family sharing a household.

By 1851, Robert (now aged 46) was living in Castleton with only his daughters Elizabeth (17) and John (11) still at home. His wife Betty is absent from the 1851 census household — she may have died between 1841 and 1851, though her death has not been traced.

Robert's death at age 74 was registered in 1878 in the Castleton district. The statutory death registration records his mother's maiden surname as Hutton, confirming his parentage.

## Life Summary

Robert Telfer, the second son of James and Elizabeth, was born at Jedburgh in 1837. He came to Australia at sixteen on the "Oliver Lang" with his brother James and sister Elizabeth. He spent his entire working life in the employ of Dr. J.W. Browne and his successor, eventually becoming manager of Moorak Station near Mount Gambier.

## Family Stories

Robert Telfer was born at Jedburgh, Scotland in 1837, the second son of James and Elizabeth. He was just sixteen when he boarded the ship "Oliver Lang" in 1854, landing in Melbourne with his brother James and sister Elizabeth. They made their way overland to South Australia and found their Uncle Francis at "Macoota" in the Adelaide Hills.

Robert's first job was working for Dr. J.W. Browne on a station in the Gawler Ranges in the north of South Australia. He later transferred to Dr. Browne's other station, "Moorak" near Mount Gambier, and that's where he settled. He was living at Moorak when he married Susan Burton on 11th April, 1865. Susan was 20, the daughter of James Burton of Claraville. The ceremony was performed by Rev. Needham at Susan's family home. The marriage certificate is almost illegible now.

Robert and Susan had five sons and four daughters.

Robert managed the German Creek section of Moorak Station for several years, then became Overseer, and eventually Manager of the whole station. After more than 50 years of service to the Browne family, ill health finally forced him to retire. He built a house he named "Carlowrie" at Yahl, near Mount Gambier, and lived there until his death.

His obituary in "The Chronicle" on 19th January, 1907, recorded: "The deceased was 72 years of age and was highly respected. He had been ailing for several years. Born in Jedburgh, Scotland, he, at the age of 16, came to South Australia. Therefore he was a colonist of 52 years standing."

The cause of death was paralysis, which had struck him repeatedly. He was described as "a man of sterling worth, of a quiet and unassuming disposition, who had made a host of friends." His funeral was conducted by Rev. Caldwell of the Presbyterian Church, and a long cortege followed him to the Mount Gambier Cemetery.

Susan Burton Telfer lived on until 1924, outliving her husband by 17 years.

*(From the Borders to the Bush, pp. 226–227)*

## Sources

- **Source:** Donald Telfer, *From the Borders to the Bush* (ISBN 0 7316 6387 X), pp. 34
- The Chronicle, 19 January 1907 — obituary

# Ruth Telfer

**Role:** Youngest daughter of Francis Charles Telfer and Amy Ellen Telfer (née Provis) — sister of Murray John Telfer
**Born:** 26 October 1931 — Saddleworth, South Australia
**Parents:** [[Francis Charles Telfer (1875–1954)]] & [[Amy Ellen Telfer (1884–1951)]]
**Brother:** [[Murray John Telfer (1924–2009)]]
**Siblings:** Francis Kelson, Clarice May, Emily Amelia, Jean, Gladys, Doris, Edwin Roy, Reginald Masters, Murray

---

## Life Summary

Ruth Telfer was the **youngest** of the ten Telfer children born to Francis and Amy Telfer. She was born at **Saddleworth**, South Australia, on 26 October 1931 — her birth name was **Pamela Ruth Telfer**, but the family called her Ruth.

Her sister Jean McMurtrie wrote in her memoir:

> \"Our youngest sister Ruth was born while we were at Saddleworth, mother was 48, and that was very hard for her, but Ruth being so much younger than the rest of us has been a real blessing to us all.\"

Ruth appears in a cherished family photograph circa 1936 at approximately age 6, riding the family horse **Duchess** with her brother Murray (then aged ~12), accompanied by the family dog.

The photograph captures a tender moment of rural childhood on the Eyre Peninsula — Ruth beaming with joy in her bob haircut and light summer top, bare legs dangling, while Murray holds the reins responsibly. Duchess, a bay with distinctive white blaze and four white socks, was clearly a beloved family horse.

Further details of Ruth's life — marriage, children, later residence — are currently being researched.

---

# Susan Burton Telfer

**Born:** 1844 | **Died:** 7 Oct 1924 (Yahl, SA) | **Spouse:** [[Robert Telfer (1835–1907)]]
